en: Preface to the Record of Chan Master Weilín’s Return to Mount Gùshān in Zhīnà, Carved [at the Request of] Chán Master Shòushān, Currently Residing at Yùlóngshān in Sàzhōu. Surrounded by a thousand disciples, his pure regulations are as solemn and orderly as those of the ancient monastic groves.
Recently, due to certain circumstances, he traveled from the provincial capital through the imperial capital, carrying with him the records of Zhīnà that he had brought along.
The *Record of Chan Master Weilín’s Return to Mount Nà* was carved onto printing blocks and circulated in the capital.

However, the preface and verses written by Chan Master Weilín for this humble monk years ago—which were composed as private remarks and thus obstructed by national regulations—were included in their entirety within the record, even though those who had heard only his reputation but not his actual teachings might have been excluded. I, [the author], revere Chan Master Shòushān.
In the midst of his rigorous and urgent journey, the Master did not forget the Dharma-gate; it is truly a joy to receive the grace of Mount Kōfukuji.
By examining the itinerary of his return in the *Gansanroku* (Record of Returning to the Mountain), I was able to learn that he visited an inn in Kashiwabara, Izumi Province, on his way back.
Once the *Gansanroku* was published, I sent my thanks; thus, through the grace of Mount Kōfukuji, I gradually came to hear of these matters.
Observing his appearance and demeanor, I recognized him as if by instinct. When I asked about his former name, he was a close friend from forty years ago;
we had met and then lost sight of one another until now, amidst our white hair and wrinkled faces. We conversed of old times and rejoiced together as in years gone by.

The Chan Master requested that I provide the preface for the *Huahui Huanshan Lu* (Record of Returning to Mount Huan) and its reasons for publication, which I have placed at the beginning of this volume. I...
Thereupon, he teased him, saying: "Today, those in China and Japan who claim to be Chan masters and publish records of their words are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds.
Is it not the case that things are valued for being rare and depreciated for being common?

The records of the various masters of this age that are of any benefit to the human world do no more than serve to cover a jar of fermented soybean paste. I wonder if your carving of this record will be any different?"
"Is that so? the Chan Master replied with a stern expression, "The Great Master of Mount Gu said: 'His words did not exceed his practice;
his practice was never less than his words. Therefore, internally he reached the land of Zhendan (China), and externally he reached Japan and Ryukyu."
Has there ever been any lapse in this? As for the words and deeds of the Great Master, they are precisely what the First Patriarch meant when he said:
"One who clarifies the Buddha-mind lineage and whose practice accords with understanding is called a Patriarch. Is it not the Great Master of Gushan who fulfills this today?
Thus, every one of his words and half-sentences is a southern-pointing needle in a sea of mist, a Northern Dipper on a night-time path. You, sir, have merged [with him].
If the contemporaries were to deliberate upon this, would it not be as if they had lost one of their eyes? Thereupon, I suddenly rose and joined my palms, saying:
"My previous words were merely in jest. To call you the Great Master of Gushan is complete and without deficiency;
it suffices now to place the Master’s own words at the beginning of this volume as the preface."

On the second day of the tenth month of the Guiyou year of the Genroku era, Dokuan Sō Genkō, a single grave within the Zen school, respectfully inscribed this preface to the *Record of Returning to the Mountains*.
The Way of the Special Transmission of the Zen School values finding the right person to pass it on. Without such transmission, how could one continue the past and open up the future?
Yet, the essential requirement for this transmission has been difficult since ancient times. As the former masters said:
"To find even one or half a person among thousands or tens of thousands who is fit to serve as a vessel—how can this be easy? Judging by today’s circumstances, this is a matter of great importance.
It relies especially upon the masters of our school, whose discernment of the Dharma is rigorous and whose wisdom and vows are vast.
They verify that those who are truly suited to the occasion are men of supramundane merit and wisdom, whose skin, flesh, marrow, and bones are linked in a single lineage with the sages of antiquity.

Only when one can shoulder this burden with naked body may the seal of mind be transmitted, so that they may uphold the fundamental principles of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and open the eyes and minds of humanity.
May these eyes be transmitted to one another so that there may be no error or confusion. In this autumn when the Dharma-vehicle is in decline, this will not merely provide small-scale assistance;
it is also intended for those who understand the Dharma to take heed. Our Master, Venerable Master Lin, personally received the seal of transmission from his late ancestor, Venerable Master Yong.
Holding the mandate of the King of Emptiness, he traversed the sea of the five turbidities, spreading the clouds of compassion and sprinkling the nectar of immortality for thirty years.
Thus it was. Examining his mind in engaging with sentient beings and benefiting them, he was like a compassionate mother tenderly caring for an infant;
yet, at the time of transmitting the Great Dharma, he firmly guarded the iron gates and would not grant any concessions.

Previously, seeing that the corruptions of the Dharma gate were like a daily descending tide whose momentum could not be turned back, he entrusted the dharma-seat to Master Jing and departed far away.
He resided at Fusha Mountain, wandering there for fourteen years, intending to spend the remainder of his life.
When Master Jing retired from his duties, the local elders of the mountain and the gentry of the capital city earnestly entreated him to return, doing so as many as several dozen times.

There were even those who knelt for a long time and wept bitterly, vowing to give their lives to urge him to set out. The Master, having no other choice, reflected that the Dharma-way of his late teacher was entrusted to him;
thus, he set aside his own will to follow the people, and suddenly rose up. When the Master returned to the mountain, ten thousand fingers rushed toward him with a roar of joy like thunder.
The monastery flagpole before the gate was resplendently raised once more. All those who ascended the hall and entered the chamber...
Furthermore, in his informal sermons (*xiaocan*) and instructions to the assembly, every word and phrase thoroughly penetrated the source and its ramifications;

every note and every thrust delved deeply into the innermost recesses. His concern for others was ever more earnest, and his desire to guide seekers was ever more urgent, yet the effect of winning over disciples remained ever more difficult to achieve.
Possessing the heart of Fengxue that shed tears, he was like a second Yangshan appearing to continue this single thread of the lineage.
The monk Mò did not know who he was. Thereupon, the disciple Fágāng requested that the Master return to the mountain and have his recorded sayings printed for circulation.

The Master joyfully consented and said to Xiyuán: "Although the lineages of the various patriarchs of the five schools from of old have long been lacking in succession, the Way remains within the Dharma-gate like the sun and moon traversing the heavens, never obscured by time. To anyone with eyes..."

Who does not see this together? I have been unworthily presiding over the Dharma altar for many years; though I have not yet encountered the karmic conditions [to propagate it], these words have not perished.
"My Way resides herein. In future generations, there will surely be those who, upon seeing this, will realize its meaning in their hearts.

Why must one receive direct oral instruction face-to-face before something can be considered one's own output? Alas! The Master’s insight was ever more profound, yet his heart grew ever more sorrowful. In the past...
Master Wuyi of Boshan once said: "In the affairs of the Zen school, what is valued is the mutual accord between heart and marrow, not the mere succession of the lineage.
If one finds the right person, whether through direct perception or hearsay, the priority and sequence are identical; there is never a point where it is severed.
If one does not find the right person, it is like adding water to milk until the flavor becomes thin, or like miswriting 'crow' three times and ending up with 'horse. How could this be preserved?"
Truly so. It is my intention that it would rather be better not to find a person than to transmit the teaching to one who is not a worthy vessel.
If one does not find a person, the lineage may indeed be severed, yet the true essence of the Way will naturally cause no harm to the Great Dharma.

If one transmits it to one who is not a worthy vessel, although the lineage may persist, the Way will become counterfeit and will, in turn, destroy its own ancestral foundation. Thus, although at that time Bozan’s Way filled the world, he never once recklessly approved of a single person.
Throughout his life, Old Man Yong was meticulous and solemn. It was not until he reached the age of eighty that he finally entrusted the True Lineage to you, Master.
He said, "There is but a single hair by which I wish to preserve the pulse of the thousand sages. How many people can truly understand such a heart? His aspirations were thus;
it is only natural that those who understood him were few. Now, Master, you are seventy-four years old; you too must cherish and be cautious.

I selected those who had not heard [these teachings] and entrusted them to them. I observed that the three masters’ resolve to protect the Dharma was in perfect accord without prior consultation, as if by matching tally-sticks.
This is precisely what the ancient worthies meant when they said: "One must be cautious with words unless one encounters a person of superior capacity. They further said:
"The talons and fangs of the Zen school, upon meeting a person of the right caliber, are brought forth; if it is a fit case, they are used together, but if not, they are immediately discarded."
This is indeed to prevent the overflow of later generations and to fortify the formidable citadel of the Dharma-gate, thereby safeguarding the wisdom-life of all sentient beings.

Is this not a great contribution to the human mind and the Way of the Dharma? Having been honored with the command to provide a preface for the opening pages, I have respectfully described the Master’s wisdom and vows through the limited perspective of one peering through a tube or measuring with a ladle. There will surely be those who appreciate these notes. This serves as the preface.
Compiled by the disciple of the Precepts, Wēnlíng Tàiháng Gōng Xīyuàn, in the first month of spring, the Wùchén year of the Kāngxī era.

The Master returned to the mountain. The Dharma-protecting officials and the fourfold assembly of the city of Fucheng requested that he ascend the hall. Clouds atop the towering peaks...
A single fragment, riding the wind, flies away and then flies back. To bring forth rain and dew is but a trivial matter;
it provokes the void to laugh until its cheeks are full. But tell me, what is it that it laughs at? After a long silence, he said: "I walk amidst the wild weeds;
he enters deep into the village. He planted his staff and descended from the seat.

At the request of the assembly of lay practitioners who protect the Dharma at Linpu, he ascends the hall. He has dwelt on this mountain for fourteen years; fourteen years have passed since he left the mountain.
Yet, in his coming and going, there is no trace. Originally, he was not elsewhere. But tell me, where is he? After a long silence, he says:
"Today, the assembly on Vulture Peak remains as it was, undispersed. He descends from the seat.
The Abbot was invited by the Chief Administrator Hong to ascend the hall. The Master took up his staff and said, "For over a dozen years, this old monk has drifted east and west;
there is no place I have not traversed—Buddha-lands, demon palaces, goat-paths, or bird-tracks—all while relying solely upon this wooden monk (the staff).
Walking, we walk together; sitting, we sit together; I have obtained my strength entirely through him. Now tell me, what is the phrase that expresses obtaining this strength?"
"How is it? Do you understand? From time to time he supports [the master] across the waters of the broken bridge; everywhere he accompanies him back to the village of the bright moon.
He struck the meditation seat once and descended.
The assembly of lay practitioners of Longjiang requested that he ascend the hall. "O friends of Longjiang, it has been over ten years since we last parted. Today..."
We met again, and our mutual affection was even more profound than before. He reverently prepared offerings for the *Gandhakuṭī* and invited me to open the Dharma assembly.
Feeling ashamed that I have no Dharma to preach, how could I answer such a noble person? I recall that in the past, a monk asked Mazu, "What is the Buddha?"
The Patriarch said, "The mind itself is Buddha. One day he further said, "Neither mind nor Buddha.
Later, Master Nanquan said, "Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing. O assembly, do these three statements of Mazu and Nanquan have degrees of intimacy or distance?
If you can discern them clearly, you may be permitted to enter the gate; if not, you cannot avoid [further instruction].
Exposing the truth: those who are close are all close; those who are distant are all distant. Why are they all distant? "In the treasury of our King, there is no such precious sword.
Even so, as for Nanquan’s saying, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing"—what, after all, is it?
Do you understand, Great Assembly? "The river is watched and remains unchanged from the vision of one's first year. This is a deception.
The Way is not the person of old, nor is it the person of today.
The Monastic Administration (Senggang) and the Abbot (Shangzuo) lead the various mountains to invite [the Master] to ascend the hall. Mount Gu does not reveal its peak;
it manifests within all dust and is encountered everywhere. Though the Buddha-eye gazes, it cannot see it. Since you have already met him, why do you not see him?
Do you understand? The stone maiden ascends the loom, the sound *ya-ya*; the wooden man beats the drum, the rhythm *dong-dong*.
Disciple Taichong Taoyuan requests the Master to ascend the hall. Fourteen years ago, the golden crow and jade hare departed into the vastness;
fourteen years later, dreamscapes and empty flowers arrive in layers. This very day, it is like the sky’s universal pervasiveness.
It is like the earth universally supporting all, like the sun universally illuminating all, and like the wind universally blowing upon all.
When one dharma is pure, all dharmas are pure; when one dharma is equal, all dharmas are equal; when one dharma is ultimate, all dharmas are ultimate.
What is called the purity of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is non-dual, indivisible, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.
At this very moment, when one has returned home and sits securely, how do you express it in a single phrase? "The crimson sun shines across the earth;
no flowers grow beneath the ocean floor. Be careful!
For the Full Repentance of the *Lanpen* (Bao-lan) to Universally Deliver Beings, invited by the virtuous men of Fucheng: Zheng Zidi, Boqin Ziliang, Taixing Mengxi, and others, he ascends the hall.
The first stroke before the sound is beyond the gaze of the thousand sages; the final pivot of opportunity leaves the myriad spirits at a loss.
A single phrase, presented directly before one’s face—he then raises his whisk and calls to the assembly, saying: "It is this very..."
Function. Apart from this function, even if you encounter someone three thousand *li* away, you must not speak of it mistakenly.

[The Master] lets out a shout and says again: "The Great Teaching of *Ullambana*, the True Wind of Gathering the Beans. Cultivated and honored for ten years, fulfilled through repentance in a single day.

May blessings accrue to parents both living and deceased, and may all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm be delivered. This is the family of the virtuous man of Fucheng, Zheng Zidi, and others."
That these relatives have united their hearts and aspirations to establish this bridge for crossing over is truly rare.
Nevertheless, as the Patriarch said: "Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin?
The Buddhas are not my Way; who is the ultimate Way? At such a time, before parents were born and before the Buddha had taken form—what is it?
[The Master] said, "At this juncture, how can one pass through to receive the news? After a long silence, he said, "There is only a favorable breeze coming upon the mat;
there are no further idle words falling into the human world. "Be careful," he added.
The Master, at the age of seventy, ascended the hall at the request of Baoshan Changxin Dashi. "This morning is the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
The stone drum is struck, its sound resonating through the void; the cassia seeds from the moon drift down with fragrance, and the pure breeze from beyond the heavens enters the chamber.

There is no need for Puhua to shake his bells, nor any use for Yunmen’s ‘The Way is Universal. From the beginning, every dharma is already perfected; let it be as it is, whether in Western Qin or Eastern Lu."

He gave a shout and descended from the seat.
At Yanping, at the request of the various mountain masters—Yuanqian, Tihu, Ruyi, Qitian, Dingsheng, and others—the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked: "In the past..."
Jinaputra said: "The Prince Nanda split his bones to return them to his father and his flesh to return them to his mother;

only then did he manifest his true body (*dharmakāya*) to preach the Dharma for his parents. [The student] asked: "What is this 'true body'? The Master said: "Realize it before your parents were born. [The student] further asked:
"I do not yet understand what kind of Dharma he preached. The Master said: "A clear breeze brushes across the white moon. [The student] said: "Today, O Master..."
"Is the preaching of the Dharma the same as or different from the Prince Nanda? The Master said, "Do not let it slip past you beneath your own feet.

He then continued: "This body is like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, or foam. I have already reached the age of seventy. When all of you come to offer congratulations, It is like seeking the tracks of a bird in the sky.
Track after track merges with empty space; Empty space contains the tracks of the bird. Space and tracks are both vast and distant— They are neither empty nor real."
"It is not real either; there is only Śūnyatā (the Void). I have come to know him. He then asked, "Tell me, what do you mean by 'I have come to know'?
After a long silence, he said, "Not knowing, not knowing," and then descended from his seat.
Lady Zhao, whose Dharma name is Chuanpu, wife of Vice-Censor Fang Xianfu of Fucheng, together with her son Fang Jing, whose Dharma name is Xingyin, requested the Master to ascend the hall.
The Master said: "The incense clouds form intricate patterns; the candle flames shine in mutual radiance. The bells and drums roar like thunder as dragons and elephants gather like clouds.
Amitāyus Tathāgata and the great assembly turn the Great Wheel of Dharma. Look toward each person’s own bare flesh."
The mountain peak stands upright like a wall ten thousand fathoms high; it is majestic, appearing ever loftier as one looks up at it, and luminous, beyond reach as one gazes upon it.
It penetrates the time before Vairocana and extends through the era after Ruci.

Suddenly, if there is a person who here and now directly realizes their place of return—like space merging with space, or water pouring into water, leaving no seams or gaps—they are of the same age as Amitābha.
The past is the same as the present; transcending the gates of quantity and number, to ascend the realm of benevolent longevity is not beyond one's capacity.

The monk stepped forward and said, "If that is so, then you, Master, are of the same age as empty space.

Today, with hair white as frost and teeth fallen out, I am once again here, prattling away, distinguishing the density and lightness of flowers in the sky, and stirring up the waves of a mirage. What business could this accomplish? After a long silence, he said:

Disciple Li Xingpu established a Huayan Universal Salvation Dharma Assembly and requested that the Master ascend the hall. "Even empty space possesses no dual characteristics;

Alas, due to following delusion and attachment to signs, one falsely perceives arising and ceasing within the dharma of non-arising, like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky.
In emptiness there are truly no flowers; they are but the deluded visions of those with cataracts.
Today, the disciple Li Xingpu, having taken refuge and observed the precepts, has given rise to a vast and great mind to cultivate the practice of universal salvation.

Taking seven weeks as his term, he desires to lead all sentient beings throughout the entire earth to ascend together through the gate of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) and collectively realize the fruit of Vairocana. "Constantly. Such merit as this is equal to the Dharma-realm and equal to empty space; how could it be measured? Nevertheless, tell me:

The Old Śākyamuni said: "The mark of the extinction of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words; it is only through the power of skillful means that it was taught for the sake of the five bhikṣus.
Then, striking the meditation staff, he said: "This very thing is not like this when arising, nor is it like this when ceasing."
It is thus. Neither arising nor ceasing is not thus. Neither non-arising nor non-ceasing is also not thus.

Only when one opens the true eye here and pierces through to the other side, and then turns back from that other side, does one finally know that arising is thus, ceasing is thus, neither arising nor ceasing is thus, and neither non-arising nor non-ceasing is thus.
Non-extinction is also like this. You must further know that within "like this" there is "not like this," and within "not like this" there is "like this.
Thus one attains great mastery over both the mundane and the supramundane. Even so, tell me: where is Master Da right now?
After a long silence, he said: "He is always here in these mountains; even the Buddha-eye cannot see him. He struck the meditation seat with his staff.
Descending from his seat at the single table, he ascended the hall.

Penglui is a land where virtuous believers abound; there, the brothers Wu Jinjing, Mingqing, and Shangqing, along with their sons and nephews, and all the men and women, old and young of the region, have come to pay their respects and offer sustenance. Introduction. Just as this Guanyin Hall has its ancient temple reopened and the Ancient Guanyin has appeared in the world, he constantly holds up the essential principles and preaches the Dharma for all of you.
What Dharma does he preach? Have you not heard it said: "The wondrous power of Guanyin’s wisdom can save the world from suffering"?
What is the wondrous wisdom of Guanyin? [The Master] picks up his staff and says: "Does the assembly see? It is ancient."
Thus one sees; now one sees thus. [The Master] struck once and said: "Do you hear? Anciently one heard thus; now one hears thus.

Hearing and seeing are perfectly luminous, never lacking in anything. If you can see through to the bottom here and gain sufficient conviction, then you will be able to take this up and carry it forth.
You will know that deluded suffering is fundamentally empty and wondrous wisdom is fundamentally present—the numinous light shines alone and brilliantly.
A magnificent legacy for ten thousand ages: every household has its Amitābha; everywhere there is Avalokiteśvara. Should this not yet be so, listen once more to a verse:
Every person possesses an ancient Avalokiteśvara, Whose marks and signs are majestic and whose compassionate vows are profound.
Day and night he emits light without ceasing; Within this, there is neither ancient nor modern. [He] strikes the meditation staff and descends from the seat.
At Zhapu on the riverbank, the Venerable Jiming and others requested that he ascend the hall. Holding up his staff, he struck it once and said:
"The spring breeze is warm; the spring grass is fragrant; the spring waters are vast; the spring dreams are long. The idle traveler yearns for his hometown.
Since he is an idle traveler, why does he yearn for his hometown? Have you not heard it said, "What is familiar is difficult to forget"? I entrust this to all of you. Look!
Even if you see it, strictly avoid deliberation or conceptualization. Then, striking the meditation seat once, he descended from the seat.
Chan Master Cuxin invited him to ascend the hall. A monk asked, "The Dharma is fundamentally beyond words; why do you speak now? The Master struck his staff.
The monk stepped forward and said, "Śākyamuni kept silent in his room and Vimalakīrti remained speechless; are these the same as your teaching today, or are they different? The Master—
The assembly gathered and expressed their appreciation. The student stepped forward and said, "The Master is a Dharma King; you possess mastery over the Dharma.

there is no need to bow your head or linger in hesitation. Indeed, when one reaches this point, what need is there to speak of Linji or Caodong? Directly!
Even if Śākyamuni himself were to arrive, he would have no choice but to be left speechless. When Bodhidharma traveled to Liang, waves arose where there was no wind;
he deserves thirty blows. Nevertheless, as for this old monk ascending the hall today—how about this?
When meeting people, speak but three parts of your words; do not yet cast forth your whole heart.
At the request of the masters Chuanzhu, Yongquan, and the others, the Master ascended the hall and said: "Today is the third day of the fourth month; the sun is at its zenith at midday.
Strike the drum for a universal invitation to behold it—the radiance pervades the entire universe.
Even so, what of those beneath the overturned basin? Do you understand? Beyond the curtain of the night-bright moon, no one arrives; the sacred tree stands far aloft, turning."
Green Shady Grove.

the patriarchs of successive generations have looked upon it but could not reach it. What more is there to say? After a long silence, he added, "Even so, there is nothing..."
"It may be said. He poured out a full measure from his basket and addressed those who seek the profound mystery: "Do not seek it elsewhere! With a shout, he descended from the seat.
On the Buddha’s Birthday, at the request of the venerable Lianju, he ascended the hall and said: "Before Śākyamuni left Tuṣita, he had already descended..."
The Imperial Palace: before even emerging from the mother's womb, one has already finished delivering all people. Proceed directly to this assembly:

boundless lands and realms, self and others, are not separated by so much as a hair’s tip; ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from the present moment of thought. If you do not understand this—
"This Dharma abides in its fixed position; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Although this is so, tell me:
whether one understands or not—of what kind of person is this a matter? (He lets out a shout.)
At Pǔtōng Monastery in Yánpíng Prefecture, the abbot Hóngkāi completed the construction of the Mahākāruṇika Hall.

Leading a gathering of fellow practitioners from the *fàngshēng* (releasing living beings) assembly, he invited [the Master] to ascend the hall. Regarding matters prior to the era of Pǔtōng: before Bodhidharma came from the West, the wind and moon were peaceful;
one could drum upon the belly and enjoy such leisure. But as for what happened after the era of Pǔtōng—how is that? [The Master] raised his staff.

He causes a jeweled palace to emerge from amidst the clouds and manifests a compassionate countenance upon the world, so that all sentient beings throughout the great earth who are in peril may find peace, and those with transgressions..."
Returning this merit, all that is sought shall be fulfilled and no goodness shall fail to arrive. Birds and fish shall all rejoice in their lives;
humans and things alike shall be moistened by its grace. Such merit flows forth from within one's own single thought of great compassion;
it is not obtained from without. Even so, tell me: what is the matter beyond the "Ordinary Age" (pǔtōng nián), and what is the matter after the "Ordinary Age"?
"The same yet different. Do you understand? When the peony blooms, it is the face of a Bodhisattva; when the palm leaves scatter, they are the head of a Yakṣa.

Together with a hundred thousand bodhisattvas, including Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, they engage in a dialogue of guest and host, question and answer, within Perfect Enlightenment.
Within this great *dhāraṇī*, immeasurable Dharma gates are manifested. It is like a wooden man singing a song or a stone maiden performing a dance.

is this merit the same as or different from that of Śākyamuni, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, the twelve great bodhisattvas, and Master Guifeng? Do you understand?
Do not say that the five notes cannot encompass it; know that the six pitch-pipes have already fully manifested it.
On the occasion of the sixtieth birthday of the lay practitioner Wang Yinglong, he requested a formal sermon. Before the birth of one’s parents, even King Wei-yin could not fathom its limits;
after the birth of one’s parents, the calendar of Emperor Xuan-yuan may measure its height and depth. You must know this.

Although this is so, consider what the Old Śākyamuni said: "Feeding a wicked person is not even a hundredth as good as feeding [a virtuous one]."

and feeding a million *srotāpannas* is not as meritorious as feeding one *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Feeding ten million *sakṛdāgāmins* is not equal to feeding one *anāgāmin*. Feeding one hundred million *anāgāmins* is not equal to feeding one *arhat*.
Feeding ten billion *arhats* is not equal to feeding one *pratyekabuddha*.
Feeding one hundred billion *pratyekabuddhas* is not equal to feeding one Buddha of the three periods of time. Feeding one thousand billion Buddhas of the three periods of time...
It is not as good as feeding one who is without recollection, without dwelling, without cultivation, and without realization.
As for how to make offerings to such a person: when the practitioner is cooking fragrant rice and it is ready, they should offer it with reverence to the One Who Is Not Hungry.

among the descendants of the lineage, who is willing to inquire into the fundamental source? All flow along with the current, chasing the waves; when will this drifting ever lead one back to the gate?

Yet his countenance remains vividly present and his true spirit has not declined; his lingering influence and remaining grace are still sufficient to inspire.

Supporting the infirm and remedying decay, acting as a stabilizing pillar against the surging waves of decline—today, Master Su, a man of venerable virtue, has traveled from over a thousand *li* away to this mountain to pay his respects at the spirit pagoda of our former teacher.
As I, the monk Pai, am but a grandson in his lineage, how shall I reveal the truth for him?
Listen further to this verse: The mountains of Min and the waters of Zhe stretch on and on; The mountains are naturally high, and the waters flow of their own accord.
"Throughout the ages and across ten thousand generations, all people have seen this. Why needlessly give rise to further sorrow?
He suddenly seized his staff, struck it once, and said, "The Master and the former teacher have arrived! The assembly bowed together, and he descended from the seat.

One aspect and one wisdom—these two superior men seek the precepts and request the Master to ascend the hall. The nature of the precepts is like empty space; those who receive them are likewise like illusions.
An illusory person and empty space face each other thus for all eternity. The light of the precepts issues from the mouth, yet it is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white.
Were one not a man of no-feelings (wuqinghan), who could perceive it directly? At this very moment, the seal and its box perfectly coincide.
"How is it when one utters a single phrase? The cassock is draped like drifting clouds; The alms bowl is spread wide like a mass of snow.
The Five Sections and Three Groups are manifested simultaneously; The bright moon and reeds—look for yourself! [He descends from his seat.]
On the Buddha’s Birthday, the Venerable Jian requested that I ascend the hall. On the eighth day of the fourth month every year, Māyā gave birth to Siddhārtha.
When spring arrives, a hundred flowers bloom; after the rain falls, a thousand peaks turn verdant. I recall how in the past Cao Shan asked Senior Monk Qiang:
"The true Dharma-body of the Buddha is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water. What do you say to this?"
He stated a principle that was appropriate, yet he insisted, "It is like a donkey looking into a well. Doushuai said, "You have spoken too much; you have only managed eight parts.
He insisted, "And what about you, Master? Doushuai said, "It is like a well looking at a donkey. Gushan said:
"A well looking at a donkey, a donkey looking at a well—how can these compare to the moon suspended in the sky, its reflection appearing in a thousand rivers"? He then took up his staff.
Zhuo said: "Today, Prince Siddhārtha has manifested his entire body within the eyes, ears, noses, and tongues of all of you, and even within your eighty-four thousand pores.
He emits great radiance and points to heaven and earth, uttering the Great Lion’s Roar: 'In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored. Do you all see him?"
If you can see this, then Śākyamuni is none other than your own self, and your own self is none other than Śākyamuni.
You appear in the world at the same time and attain Buddhahood on the same day.
All-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) is pure, non-dual, indivisible, without distinction, and uninterrupted. If it were otherwise, one would not see the person who fills the valleys and ditches. From...
He applied gold leaf to the surface of the teaching platform, struck it once, and descended from his seat.
He then ascended the hall and said: "The Honorable Grandee Han Gong, Layman Taian, has reached the age of seventy-two.

For over forty years he has maintained a lifelong vegetarian fast, reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily to illuminate the ground of his mind. Today he has entered the mountain to offer this memorial service."
I request the elder monk to ascend the seat, to proclaim the intent of the Buddha and bestow it universally upon the great assembly, thereby establishing a causal connection with Prajñā.
Do you understand? Every person possesses their own Vajra; from antiquity to the present, it has flowed forth without a moment’s forgetfulness. It is neither word, nor letter, nor principle;
it pervades space and the world, never hidden away. Therefore, the Elder Śākyamuni exerted his full strength to break through [the delusion], saying:
Of all classes of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;

whether possessing form or formless; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation. In this way, I shall liberate immeasurable, incalculable, and...

"Regarding 'sentient beings at the periphery': in reality, there are no sentient beings who attain *nirvāṇa*. The Venerable Dazhu of the Tang Dynasty explained: the nine classes of sentient beings are fully present within the single mind;
they are formed as they act. Ignorance constitutes birth from an egg; being enveloped by afflictions constitutes birth from a womb;
being moistened by the water of craving constitutes birth from moisture; and the sudden arising of afflictions constitutes miraculous birth (*upapāduka*). Awakening is precisely this..."
The Buddha said: "Those who are deluded are called 'sentient beings. A Bodhisattva regards only the mind of every thought-moment as sentient beings.

If one realizes that the essence of the mind in every thought-moment is empty, this is what is meant by 'delivering sentient beings. The wise deliver those who have not yet taken form within the primordial limit;
since that which has not yet taken form is empty, they know that in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. "Great Assembly, the World-Honored One speaks thus."
"Master Dazhu commented thus; today this old monk proclaims it thus: Is it one's own vajra, or is it not one's own vajra?
Do you understand? 'The one who knows does not need frequent mention; the wise must know how to nod their heads in the dark.
[He] struck his staff and descended from the seat."
When Layman Shaoxi of Shaowu invited the assembly for a meal and requested that the Master ascend the hall, a monk asked: "The paths of sage and ordinary are cut off, leaving no stages;
through sudden awakening, the profound mystery opens the gate of non-duality. Within this gate of non-duality, who is it that emerges? The Master replied:
"Where do you, Venerable Sir, currently plant your feet? The monk stepped forward and said: "The local scenery of the original ground transcends all things; within it, one is alone..."

[The Master] revealed the wondrous and profound pivot. The Teacher said, "You are still a man outside the gate. The Master then said, "In the ground of ultimate reality, not a single speck of dust is established;

within the gateway of myriad practices, not a single dharma is abandoned. Today, the lay practitioner Wang Shaohui cooks riceless rice, fills a bottomless bowl, and offers it to the Compassionate Honored Ones of the three periods and the pure assembly of the six harmonies. This is the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā)."
Mindfulness is perfectly luminous; one enters directly into the body of the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means.
Even so, tell me: how does one make offerings to that single person? The wooden child constantly presents round fruits;
the stone woman eternally holds the *padma* flower.
On the occasion of the mid-autumn festival for the Universal Deliverance (Pudu), the disciples Ge Cijin, Guo Bingwen, Guo Zhaoyuan, and others requested the Master to ascend the hall.
The Master said: "The entire assembly has united their hearts to perform this Universal Deliverance; three years have passed, and we rejoice that the work is accomplished.
May all four debts of gratitude and the beings of the three realms together ride upon the power of the Dharma to realize non-arising. But tell me, what is this 'non-arising'?"

“Understood? Does the great assembly understand? On the fifteenth day of the seventh month every year, all Buddhas are filled with joy, and the monastic community each enjoys their *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence).
If you recognize that the food is originally rice, what then? Once recognized, how is it? ‘In heaven and on earth, one is worthy of offerings.
[He lets out a shout and says: ‘The one who eats this *huoluo* (mixed) meal is not you.”
On the occasion of the sixtieth birthday of the Five Lay Practitioners led by Sun Kui, the Master was invited to ascend the hall to offer a meal for the monks.
The Master said: "The spiritual source is inexhaustible; it has been thus from antiquity to the present. In humans, it is the same as humanity; in heaven, it is the same as heaven.
He held up his staff and said, "Tell me, how is it upon the tip of this old monk’s staff? He struck the ground once and said, "Today is the Tathāgata Amitāyus."

Here, for the sake of all people, he turns the Great Wheel of Dharma. The immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lifespans directed toward the Way exist only within this present single kṣaṇa.
Within one kṣaṇa lies immeasurable lifespan; so it is with every kṣaṇa as well.

With such a lifespan, he universally bestows predictions of enlightenment upon all sentient beings of the great earth at once—like the sky universally covering all, like the earth universally supporting all, leaving nothing out.
Just as today, when the Elder Layman Kuai invited the Sangha for a meal and requested the Dharma, how would you express this single phrase:
"Receiving blessings in accordance with the occasion"? "The fragrant breeze has already arrived; The lofty trees are in full, lush splendor. [He] stood upright, leaning on his staff.
The Master descended from his seat.
On the occasion when Chan Master Dingmo was ordaining a disciple to leave the household life and receive the precepts, he requested the Master to ascend the hall. The Master said:

"Now, as for those who leave the household life, they leap forth from the nature of the three dependencies and join the ranks of the Three Jewels as honored ones. They don the robes of the field of merit and shave the hair of affliction."

Having personally received the precepts, one is utterly liberated from worldly toil; practicing the Brahma-conduct life after life and birth after birth, one delivers sentient beings wherever they may be, vowing to ascend to the fruits of sainthood and ultimately realize Bodhi.
Although this is so, how shall one express the single phrase of standing tall and independent upon the Diamond Ground?
Let the five turbidities be as deep and bottomless as they may—[the Diamond Ground] is difficult to defile.
A lotus emerging from the pond of the mind.
The Venerable Tōshō requested him to ascend the hall. The Master said: "The Venerable Tōshō has respectfully come to request the Dharma; the bright mirror of the mind is set squarely upon its stand.
The holy and the ordinary of the ten realms all manifest their reflections therein; within this, not even a speck of dust can remain. Just as it is now—"
Today, surrounded by the fourfold assembly at the Dharma seat, with eyes wide open, ears alert, and minds clear, listen as this old monk speaks of the yellow road and white path.
Tell me, is this a reflection or not? Do you understand? The myriad phenomena of the forested world are not other than it;
their inherent radiance pervades the nine realms.
On the occasion of the Sixtieth Birthday of the Venerable Cimen, the Master ascended the hall and said:
"Before entering the womb, empty space could not contain him; after emerging from the womb, a mustard seed has room to spare.
That which a mustard seed can contain with room to spare is what empty space cannot contain; that which empty space cannot contain is what a mustard seed contains with room to spare. Herein—"
When you see through to the bottom and can carry it upon your shoulders, the boundless realms of all lands—self and other—are not separated by so much as a hair’s tip;

ten eons of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from this very moment of thought. If it were otherwise, it would be like building a mountain that reaches nine *ren* high, yet failing to weigh out the thousand *jin* of soil required to complete it.
The disciple of Yanping Puguang Temple, Mukan Miqin Buqi, together with the assembly, requested the precepts and invited the Master to ascend the hall.
The Master said: "The precept of the fundamental source and original nature is inherently pure; it resides within a single thought-moment of each person.

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, it remains ever indestructible, like the brilliant sun shining upon the void. Great assembly, you must know that although the nature of this precept is originally present,"
Revealed through the teacher, one ascends the hall for the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and instruction in dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Step by step, one is within the Vajra-maṇḍala; matter by matter, it is the ground of the mind of Samantabhadra. By means of this, one benefits oneself to ultimately realize Bodhi;

by means of this, one benefits sentient beings to universally deliver them with equanimity. Thus it is said: "When sentient beings receive the Buddha-precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas. Their rank is identical [to that of the Buddhas].
The Great Awakening has been attained; you are truly the sons of all Buddhas. Do you all yet believe yourselves? Do you all yet accept yourselves?
"I do not dare to look down upon you; you shall all become Buddhas. Descend from your seats.
On the Buddha’s Birthday, Huang Konggu, a filial scholar-official from Wenling, requested the Master to ascend the hall on behalf of his late mother, Lady Liu Benzhi.
The Master said: "Every person’s father is King Śuddhodana; every person’s mother is Queen Māyā.

Just observe that every year on the eighth day of the fourth month, everywhere fragrant waters bathe the Prince. When a single offering is presented, all Buddhas arrive together. [He] offered a meal...
That a single monk is the universal assembly of a thousand sages is neither a marvelous exercise of supernatural powers nor a matter of natural law;

it is simply the inherent nature and merit of the person themselves. Today, Huang Konggu, a filial scholar-official, on behalf of his late mother, Lady Liu, requests the Dharma and the reception of the precepts.
As we celebrate this feast, how can one express it in a single phrase? "Mother and son share the same heart as they cultivate merit."
Wisdom! May the legacy of this lineage remain fragrant for a hundred generations. Cherish this.

Within the sandalwood grove there are no other trees; dense and profound, the lion dwells there. Foxes, wolves, and jackals have all hidden their tracks; this single piece of true wind pervades heaven and earth.
What is this "single piece of true wind"? Have you not seen what the Patriarch said? "The Dharma of the mind is formless..."
It fills the ten directions. When it is in the eyes, it is called seeing; when in the ears, it is called hearing; when in the nose, it smells fragrances;

when in the tongue, it engages in discourse; when in the hands, it grasps and seizes; when in the feet, it moves and runs. It manifests everywhere, encompassing all within the dust-motes of the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*;

yet when withdrawn, it is contained within a single minute atom (*paramāṇu*). Those who recognize it know it to be Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*prāṇa*). O virtuous ones, if you can truly recognize the Buddha...
As for the nature (*dhātu*): it is that which maintains the monastic community, bears the responsibility for the great assembly, establishes the Triple Gem, and propagates the Mahāyāna.
Every one of these flows forth from within *prajñā*. If one does not recognize Buddha-nature, then every matter is a functioning of conceptual consciousness (*vijñāna*).
To employ conceptual consciousness is for conceptual consciousness to gather; to practice *prajñā* is for *prajñā* to dwell together. It is like a sandalwood grove—[only] sandalwood.
It is surrounded by *tán* trees; it is surrounded by thickets of thorns. This is certainly not false.
Since the time our late teacher, the Venerable Old Master of Boshan, first founded Gushan, more than sixty years have passed. The true wind has not fallen, and the ancient path still endures.
I only wish that each and every one of you gentlemen will open a mind of singular penetration and exert a will that transcends the common crowd, so as to clarify—
The nature that has existed from the beginning gives rise to the merit of non-action; you shall continue the fragrant traces of former worthies and serve as an excellent guide for future students.
To lead those from the four quarters to return together to the ground of enlightenment—this is what I hope for most earnestly.

At such a time as this, how would you express the saying: "Those of the same sound respond to one another; those of the same breath seek one another"? Listen further to this verse: "The Buddha-nature resides in every person."
"Originally they are the same. The six functions are perfectly luminous; whether empty or not empty, with a single thought one turns the mechanism and the whole body is revealed.
He suddenly called out to the assembly. The assembly all raised their heads, whereupon he said: "The moon of wisdom in the sky of nature is exactly in the center. Take care!"

this body is a vajra-body, suchness itself, unchanging and immutable. Time and seasons fundamentally do not shift, for the span of one's life is eternal."
What limit can there be? Day and night it emits radiance; from ancient times to the present, it has always been brilliantly resplendent.
Now tell me, where is the True Person of No Station right now? (He raises his whisk and says: "Does the assembly see? (He gives a shout and descends from his seat.)

‘After the monkey embraces its child and returns to the green peaks, the bird carries a flower and drops it before the emerald crags. What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, “It is right before your eyes. The monk pressed further, “As for Fayan saying, ‘For thirty years I took this only as an objective realm,’ what does that mean?”
"How so? The Master said, "Even the mind cannot grasp it. The monk bowed. The Master then said: "The sentient beings and the Buddhas are fundamentally the same;

the myriad phenomena and the vast cosmos are within a single mirror. Blessings arise from the ground of the mind; as life after life passes, the fruits of blessing naturally become ever more magnificent.
He raised his whisk and called to the assembly, "What is this? After a long silence, he said, "The five eyes cannot behold it."
"Behold! Ten thousand ages are naturally void and luminous. [The Master] strikes the sounding block and descends from his seat.

"The orthodox lineage of Buddhas and Patriarchs, the eyes of humanity and devas—this does not come from elsewhere; it flows forth directly from within this very state. As for the matter within this state..."
"How is it? He held up his staff and said, "This very thing is called a staff. To call it 'salt and plum' is to disturb the primal soup;

not to call it a staff is to abandon the waves to seek the water. Finally, how is it? He struck the floor three times and said, "Constantly indestructible through all ages, serving as a bridge and raft for every generation. He struck once more and descended from the seat.

A General Discourse for the Congregation. The Master said: "The Buddha appeared in the world; the Patriarchs came from the West; the altars for selecting Buddhas exist everywhere."
"Open! Throughout the winter and summer retreats, one exhausts the ultimate matter; upon a single awakening, one passes the examination of the empty mind and returns with honors.
Is there anyone like this? After a long silence, he said: 'In the past, the Great Master Bodhidharma saw that this land possessed the great capacity for the Mahayana.'"
He therefore came specifically by sea to point directly at the human mind and see one's nature to become a Buddha. But tell me, what is this "pointing directly"?
Have you not seen when Emperor Wu of Liang asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have had scriptures printed, temples built, and monks ordained beyond counting;
what merit and virtue do these bring? The Patriarch replied, "There is no merit. Is this not pointing directly?
[The Master] pointed his finger. He asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Patriarch said, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. The Emperor said, "Who is it that faces me?
The Patriarch said, "I do not know. Is this not direct pointing? The Second Patriarch asked, "My mind, your disciple, is not yet at peace."
The Second Patriarch requested the Master to settle his mind. The Master said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall settle it for you.
The Second Patriarch replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable. The Master said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. Is this not a direct pointing?

Since that time, through the transmission of the robe for six generations and the emergence of the five schools, none have failed to employ this Way to guide others. Therefore, those who have realized their nature and attained the Way are beyond counting.
The ultimate limit. For example, when the Sixth Patriarch asked Nanyue from where he had come, Nanyue replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch asked, "What thing comes like this?
When Master Qingyuan Si was dwelling with the community discussing the Way, the Master remained silent.
Layman Pang asked Shitou, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as its companion? Shitou covered [Pang's] mouth with his hand.
[The monk] spoke. He asked Mazu again, and Mazu said, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River in a single mouth, and then I will tell you.
A monk asked Mazu, "What is the Buddha? Mazu said, "This very mind is the Buddha. He asked Yunmen, and Yunmen said, "A dried-up shit-stick. He also said, "Three pounds of flax.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou—
It is said that before the courtyard cypress tree, Linji asked Huangbo three times about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times he was struck with the staff.
All of the above are instances where the ancients cut open their bellies and gouged out their hearts to hold [the truth] face-to-face and hand it over with both hands.
Alas, later generations have lacked discernment. Upon hearing it said that "the cypress tree," they take the cypress tree as their livelihood;
upon hearing it said that "a dried-up dung pellet," they seek it out within the dung pellet; upon hearing it said that "mind itself is Buddha," they give rise to deluded thoughts within the mind.
This is what is called "marking the boat to find the sword"—they miss the point of the ancients and fail them grievously.
Therefore, this matter must be entrusted only to a man of worldly-transcending merit and wisdom who is capable of bearing it;
only such a person may enter and practice it. If one is not that person, there is no place to stand even outside the triple gate, let alone entering within.
Thus, when one looks upon this matter, it appears truly difficult, truly difficult. Nevertheless, if one is a person with blood beneath their skin, [it is otherwise].
The Han man, upon hearing these words, felt a piercing pain that reached to the very marrow of his bones.
He gave rise to a true and sincere aspiration, vowing resolutely to clarify this one point and to bring to an end the birth and death that has remained unresolved since immeasurable kalpas.

He resolved to awaken to the self-mind that has remained unawakened since immeasurable kalpas, to continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom, to transmit and transform for the future, and to repay the Buddha’s profound kindness. If he were able to...
With such a solemn vow, I dare to guarantee that ultimate accomplishment will be achieved. Therefore, an ancient worthy said: "The sages and worthies were all ordinary people;
why not follow their example and practice? He further said: "Since antiquity, the great masters have traveled to various regions seeking the Way.

Although they lacked any specific name for their 'exertion of effort,' when the Great Matter was not yet clarified, their single mind remained fixed on the Way, with every thought-moment [directed toward it]."

He was unwilling to let it pass. Thus, there came a day when he attained awakening and clarity. It was not until the Song Dynasty that the teaching of using a "critical phrase" (*huatou*) as a means of practice first emerged.
At that time, people were simply instructed to hold up a critical phrase and examine what its underlying principle is.
For instance, Chan Master Dahui frequently taught people to contemplate the phrase, "The dog has no Buddha-nature," asserting that the entire great earth is [this very point].
This single word "Mu. When ignorance and afflictions manifest right before you, bring it up once and say, "Mu.
It is like pouring a ladle of cold water into a hundred-boiling cauldron; immediately, there is coolness. This is roughly how one brings up the *huatou*.
Later, the venerable masters further instructed people to give rise to a profound state of doubt, using that doubt to trigger awakening.
This is the pivot. Thus it is said: "To have no doubt regarding words and phrases is a great affliction. Great doubt leads to great awakening;
small doubt leads to small awakening; no doubt leads to no awakening. Those who have attained the Way through such practice are beyond counting.

It was not until the beginning of the Yuan dynasty that the doctrine of "dead-work" (si-gongfu) emerged. Masters such as Xueyan and Gaofeng, having themselves practiced dead-work, [instructed others accordingly].
Master Shangwu was enlightened; therefore, he constantly demonstrated the practice of "dead effort" (*si gongfu*) to others. Many who relied upon it attained awakening and realized the Way.

In short, if one possesses a single piece of sincere resolve regarding birth and death, there will naturally be a corresponding resonance. Thus it is said: "There is no secret method for practicing Chan;

it simply requires that the matter of birth and death be urgent. To the degree that it is urgent, there is that much practice. If it is ten times as urgent," [the practice will be ten times as effective].
Then there will be ten parts of true effort. If one does not know that there is this great matter of birth and death, such a person has no share in the practice of Chan.
Although this is so, there is one who does not fall into birth and death; after all, what is his countenance? After a long silence, he said:
"The assembly has stood for a long time; take care."
Addressing the assembly, the Master said: "Nanquan said: 'It is not the mind; one who has no pupil in the eye sees it truly. It is not a Buddha;
the hundreds of thousands of marks and signs are difficult to manifest. It is not an object; the thousand hands of Great Compassion cannot touch it.
When the ancients proclaimed it in this way, and I, the old monk, judge it in this way, it is just as Master Dahui said: 'Like a person from Fuzhou.'"
I have eaten lychees; having peeled the skin and removed the pit, I offered them into your mouth, yet you simply do not know how to swallow them.

This old monk says that even if you could swallow them down, you must also be able to spit them back out. Even if you were perfectly clear about swallowing and spitting, only then would it be appropriate to receive a blow of the staff upon entering the gate of Gushan.
Let this matter rest for now; as for the fact that since the commencement of the retreat in the hall...
Half a month has passed. Have you all ever carefully examined and scrutinized that which is most essential within your own domain?
What is this most essential matter within your own domain? Previously, I brought up the two characters for "birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra*).
Is this not a matter of vital importance to oneself? Furthermore, he has brought forward a person who does not fall into birth and death for you to investigate;
is this not a matter of vital importance? Nowadays, people treat the two words "birth and death" as mere lip service, regarding them as commonplace.
They assume this body can be preserved for a hundred years, making plans only upon their own skulls.
Do not fail to realize that the demon of impermanence (*anityatā*) does not spare you for even a single thought-moment; once its fangs are bared, one departs forever for a thousand ages.
Will this not mean that one’s entire life has passed in vain? If you think, "I shall emerge again to investigate Zen and study the Way within the Buddha-dharma," I fear it cannot be guaranteed.
However, if you truly know that there is one who does not fall into birth and death, [then you will understand].
Having personally resolved my indignation, I have investigated and clarified this matter with earnest persistence; how could I ever allow myself to be complacent?

It is like a person who recognizes that there is a treasure trove within their own room; they will naturally take up a handleless hoe and dig here and there until, suddenly, they strike upon it—*awk!*—and realize, "Ah!
It was all along right here. Having attained this great utility, they experience a lifelong sense of joy and fulfillment.
It is truly lamentable that people of these times, upon picking up a mere fragment of tile or rubble, claim it to be pure gold.
They give rise to thoughts of wonder and thoughts of sufficiency; how can they not bring about their own ruin? Nevertheless, as the ancients said:
"It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. Now tell me, is this statement pure gold or is it tile and rubble? The Mandarin-Duck Pillow.
[The Master] shed tears in two streams; half were from thinking of you, and half were from resenting you.
"Be careful," he said, addressing the assembly. The Master continued: "The other day, when I raised the two characters 'birth' and 'death,' I had not yet cut them off completely.
Today, I cannot help but once more entangle the assembly in a web of words. Long ago, there was a monk who asked Master Touzi: 'When the four mountains press in from all sides...'"
At that time, [the monk] asked, "How is it? Touzi said, "The five aggregates are all empty. "Assembly, tell me:
when Touzi answered in this way, was it Chan or was it Teaching? If you say it was Chan, what difficulty is there in understanding 'the five aggregates are all empty'?
If you say it was Teaching, how could 'the five aggregates are all empty' be easy to understand? You must know that the five aggregates are the four mountains; the four mountains..."
These are precisely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Once one truly realizes that the five aggregates are all empty, what "four mountains" could there possibly be?
Therefore, when the Elder Avalokiteśvara practiced Prajñā at that time, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty;

thus, everything was settled once and for all. What further suffering or calamity could there be to be delivered from? If one says he "delivered others from suffering and calamity," it becomes merely a redundant expression (*adhivacana*). Now...
People of the time merely carry these words along with them in their thoughts, paying no attention at all. Is this not lamentable? An ancient worthy composed a verse:
"A single void atop the mountain of the five aggregates— Is this void and the five aggregates one or two? Entering and exiting through the same gate, they do not meet;
If they were to meet, the skull would shatter into dust. For immeasurable kalpas, one has lived in a rented house; A hired laborer speaks of what he does not do."
"Ma! To the very end, one does not recognize the true host. How is the true host to be recognized? Nowadays, when people are asked about this true host, everyone says, 'I know it.

Yet ten out of twenty merely identify with that which is currently manifest—this discerning, luminous, and numinous awareness that exists when awake but is absent when one falls asleep, that exists when alive but is gone when dead."
It is simply non-existent. Little do they realize that this faculty of discernment and awareness has been the very root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas.
To mistake it for the true master is not a great error? This is precisely what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* denounces as "mistaking a thief for one's son. Therefore, Master Changsha said:
"Those who study the Way fail to recognize the Real, solely because they have from of old identified with the consciousness-spirit. It is non-existent.

The root of birth and death since immeasurable kalpas—fools call this the "original person. Furthermore, there is another class who cite the words of the Patriarchs to authenticate their own views, saying:
"In the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing; in the hand it grasps and seizes; in the foot it moves and runs.
It manifests everywhere, encompassing all lands as numerous as grains of sand, yet when withdrawn, it is contained within a single minute atom. Those who recognize it call it Buddha-nature."
If you do not recognize it, you call it "vital spirit" (*jinghun*). If you truly do recognize it, to call it "Buddha-nature" (*foxing*) is no exaggeration.
If this is not yet the case, you are merely a fellow who dabbles with vital spirits; what common ground for conversation could there be?
You must know that at that time, although the Patriarch’s words were like clarified butter (*tīhú*), they were also like poison. Is there anyone capable of discerning between them?
If you cannot discern [the truth], listen further to these verses: "Clarified butter and poison are both extracted together;
How many men can recognize the true? Seizing empty space, one strikes the very marrow; After striking it out, what then? After a long silence, he said:
"The nostrils remain as they were, resting upon the upper lip. "Be careful! (Zhenzhong)
The Master opened the precepts for the assembly, saying: "Virtuous ones, most of you have traveled hundreds or thousands of miles, crossing over streams and mountains from afar to seek the precepts.
Yet, by this very thought, you have already attained the precepts. This is called the precept of the primordially pure self-nature. It is without observance and without violation;
without defilement and without purity; without gain and without loss. All myriad virtues are fully present, requiring no further effort."

One seeks it externally, yet for immeasurable kalpas one has been internally entangled by fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana*) and externally deluded by objective conditions (*viṣaya-pratyaya*), unable to break through.
Today, as soon as you give rise to a single thought of purity and seek the precepts, these precepts will manifest in their entirety before you.
It is like clouds parting and the moon emerging, its pure light shining everywhere; what obstruction could there be? For this original source—
The precept of intrinsic nature is also called the Vajra Jewel Precept, meaning it is firm and indestructible.
It is also called the unconditioned essence of the precept, meaning it does not arise from conditions but is manifested through them.

Thus, the Buddhas of the three periods—those who have recited, those who are reciting, and those who will recite—all recite this precept. The Bodhisattvas of the three periods—those who have studied, those who are studying, and those who will study—all study this precept.

Thus it is. The three masters transmit and receive this precept; the seven assemblies of the Sangha bear witness to this precept. Outside of the precepts, there are no further precepts—what other precepts could there be?

O virtuous ones, if you can see through to the bottom here and gain full conviction, you will know that the *karmavācanā* performed upon the platform is the entire Vajra Bodhimanda, and that spreading out the bowl and donning the robes is entirely the ground of the mind of Śākyamuni.

Everywhere the light of the precepts shines; from time to time the Dharma of the precepts circulates. It may be said that when sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
Once their rank is equal to that of Great Enlightenment, they are truly the children of all Buddhas.

O virtuous ones, having arrived at this point—like an eighty-year-old man entering the examination hall—is this not a momentous occasion? You must give rise to a heart of true reality. Give rise to...
With a vast mind, one generates the resolve to cross over birth and death, the resolve to deliver all sentient beings, and the resolve to seek unexcelled bodhi.
Having received these wondrous precepts, from this very day until the attainment of Buddhahood, one proceeds directly ahead without any deviation or detour.
If one can make such a solemn vow, only then is one called a true child of the Buddha and a true bhikṣu.

Furthermore, if one’s mental conduct is not authentic, if one’s power of aspiration is not vast, and if one is even careless regarding one’s robes and alms bowl, merely following the crowd to ascend the altar—then although one may plant a seed upon this very ground of reality, if one hopes for flowers to bloom and fruit to ripen, one does not know when that will ever happen.
O worthy ones, a human body is difficult to obtain; the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter. In a single thought-moment...

Turning the light back, one immediately ascends to the stage of the precepts. Do you still understand? Listen further to this repeated verse: "The precept of the original source and inherent nature is pure;
The great jewel has long been obscured by dust and unrecognized. In a single thought of a pure mind, it manifests in its entirety;
The black dog and the white ox laugh and smile. The assembly has stood for a long time; take care.

On the eve of the year of Yi-chou, he addressed the assembly: "All sentient beings throughout the great earth who have not yet attained the fruits of sagehood remain entirely within the realm of ordinary persons.
Throughout the three hundred and sixty days of a year, during each of the twelve hours of every day, whether lifting a foot or taking a step, opening the mouth or moving the tongue,"
Every arising thought and every stirring of the mind that does not accord with principle is, without exception, a transgression.
If these transgressions possessed a substantial nature, even the entirety of the realm of empty space could not contain them;

however, because their nature is empty, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, opened the gate of repentance to enable beings to reform their past and cultivate the future, thereby returning to original purity. But tell me, how does one repent? Samantabhadra—
The *Contemplation Sutra* states: "The ocean of all karmic obstructions arises entirely from deluded thoughts.
If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). But tell me, how does one contemplate the true mark?

Formerly, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, five hundred bhikṣus attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five supernormal powers, yet they had not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). By means of their knowledge of past lives...
Each of them, reflecting upon their past lives, recalled the various crimes they had committed, such as killing their fathers and harming their mothers;
within their own minds, each harbored doubts and was unable to enter into the profound Dharma.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, grasped a sharp sword in his hand and pressed it against the Tathāgata. The World-Honored One then said to Mañjuśrī: "Stop, stop! Do not..."
"You should commit the act of parricide; do not harm me. If I am harmed, it will be an act of harming the virtuous.
"Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning you have had no self or person; it is only through the internal mind that you perceive a self or person.

When the internal mind arises, 'I' am necessarily harmed, and this is precisely what is called 'harming. Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus realized for themselves that their original mind is like a dream.
"It is like a phantom. Within a dream or a phantom, there is no self or person, nor are there parents who give birth or those who are born.
Thereupon, five hundred bhikṣus praised him with one voice, saying: 'Mañjuśrī, Great Sage of Wisdom, you have profoundly penetrated the very source of the Dharma.
Though you personally grasped a sharp sword and pressed it against the body of the Tathāgata, the sword and the Buddha were likewise identical; they are a single mark without duality.'"
Phenomenal marks are unarisen; how, then, can there be killing within them? Great Assembly, tell me:
how far apart were those five hundred bhikṣus—who in their past lives killed their fathers and harmed their mothers—and Mañjuśrī, who grasped a sword and coerced the Tathāgata?
If you can see into this point here, with a single stroke you will cut through both ends. Since the marks of merit cannot be found, where could one look for sin to come from?
If this is not yet so, for now, seek realization within the tangle. O assembly, how excellent is the World-Honored One’s saying:
“Stop, stop! Do not respond; do not act in opposition. How excellent is Mañjuśrī’s saying: “From the very beginning, you have been without self or person.”
It is simply because one perceives a self or a person within the inner mind that when the inner mind arises, "I" am inevitably harmed; this is precisely what is called "harm.

How excellent it is that these five hundred bhikṣus awakened to their own fundamental mind as being like a dream and like an illusion—within this dream and illusion, there is no self or person, nor are there parents who give birth or those who are born.
Again, how excellent it is that the Buddha is like a sword: his single mark is non-existent.
There are two [aspects]: signlessness and non-arising. Within this, how could there be killing?

If you can see through these four excellent words and gain conviction in them, then the affliction-obstructions, karma-obstructions, and retribution-obstructions from immeasurable kalpas will be purified on the spot.
It is like hot water melting ice; in a single thought-moment, one is transformed into supreme awakening. How much more so for those who practice and attain realization!

If, however, one does not believe or understand, but instead indulges their own ignorant sentiments to commit various transgressions without any sense of dread, I fear they will lose their human form beneath the *kāṣāya*.
This is something that cannot even be compared to the hells—how tragic this is!
On the Lantern Festival of the Bingyin year, he addressed the assembly: "Night after night, the lamp is lit to transcend the world; day after day, the sun’s face radiates light.
Of the more than three hundred days in a year, let us, gentlemen, deliberate together. But tell me, what is it you are deliberating about? After a long silence, he said:
"Heaven and earth are dark and yellow; the universe is vast and ancient.

[The Master] addressed the assembly, saying: "After the ancients attained the Way, some spent their days in the company of the community, while others secluded themselves in deep mountains to nurture their realization."
I only fear that my name and traces might fall among the common people. Once the fruit has ripened and its fragrance wafted abroad, the dragons and devas will push me forth;
to then abandon myself and follow others is truly a matter of necessity. How could this be like those people of today, who, having heard and seen but little, only fear that others do not know them?

To be so anxious to sell oneself to others reveals that one’s aspirations and character are base and vulgar. Furthermore, when people of antiquity went on pilgrimage, it was solely for the purpose of meeting others.
Those who had not yet attained realization would seek instruction morning and evening, seeking even a single word or half-phrase to awaken their fundamental nature.
Those who had already attained realization sought teachers to resolve their doubts and establish the definitive meaning of their school. How could they have been like people of the present day?
They merely set foot upon name-and-form (nāmarūpa), entering one thicket and emerging from another, yet entirely lacking a sincere heart that seeks the Dharma;
they simply follow the crowd for meals and spend their days wandering aimlessly. Such has been the history of the rise and fall of the Buddha-dharma.
Today, I specifically bring forth for the great assembly the meeting between Dongshan and Master Mi, who visited Yinshan.

I shall compose a brief account of this causal connection as a proclamation, so that the wise may know shame and recognize their own failings, and upon seeing the worthy, may strive to emulate them, thereby avoiding falling into vulgar custom and bringing their lifelong efforts to naught. It is said:

Long ago, there was an elder who, having received the essential meaning from Mazu, lived in seclusion at Longshan in Tanzhou for an unknown number of years; no one knew of his presence. One day, Dong...
Shan and his senior master Mi traveled together. As they passed by the foot of the mountain, they saw vegetable leaves flowing down from a stream in the ravine.
The two men said to one another, "This deep mountain is uninhabited; how can there be vegetable leaves following the current? Is there perhaps a practitioner of the Way dwelling here?"
Thereupon, they discussed cutting through the weeds to catch a glimpse of the wind. After traveling five or seven *li* along the stream, they suddenly saw a thatched hut.

Inside was an elderly master with a frail form and unusual appearance. They set down their luggage and paid their respects. The old master said, "This mountain has no path; from where have you *kalyāṇamitra*s come?
(The commentary says: "From the void he cast his direct hook. Dongsan said, "Setting aside for a moment the matter of 'no path,' from where did you, Master, come?"
He went back to the fishing spot. The old master said, "I do not come from the wandering clouds" (meaning: I do not seek outside).
