Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised a case: A monk asked an ancient worthy, "Is there still Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs?
The ancient worthy said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs?

The ancient worthy said, "A strange stone, its shape like a tiger; a pine tree scorched by fire, its form like a dragon. The Master said, "It is clear in every instance; it is manifest in every thing."
This is so. Thus, it was not that the ancient worthies lacked [the Dharma]. Yet, as for the Buddha-dharma of deep mountains and rocky cliffs, it remains separated from us by a mountain.
If someone were to ask Gushan today, "Is there still Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs? he would likewise answer, "There is."
If someone asks, "What is the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky precipices? simply tell them: "It is profound, firm, remote, and secluded;
no one can reach it. Now tell me, is this the same as the ancients, or is it different? If you can discern this, I grant that you possess the eye of wisdom.
Addressing the assembly, he raised a case: A monk asked Yunmen, “What is the One Great Canon of Teachings? Yunmen said, “I speak in response to the one.
On another day, a monk asked, “When it is neither the mechanism before one’s eyes nor the matter before one’s eyes, what then?
Yunmen said, “I speak upside down. The Master said: “What is ‘the one’ that can be responded to? And what is ‘responding’ that can respond to the one? Furthermore—
First, what is it that can be overturned? What is this overturning that can be overturned?
The Old Man of Shaoyang, out of compassion, had his talk of "falling into the weeds. Today at Gushan, it is not so. If someone asks, "What is the Great Canon of Teachings?
simply say to him, "In the tea, in the rice. If he asks, "Is it not... [the response follows].
"How is it when the present function is not the present matter? To him he said, "In the eye; in the ear.
Tell me, is this the same as Yunmen, or is it different? Do you understand? It is easy to distinguish flour from snow, but difficult to discern soot within ink.
Take care!

On the occasion of the Summer Retreat, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Every year on the fifteenth day of the fourth month, regardless of whether one is in India or China, for three months one observes the *kaṭhina* and protects living beings;
every household carefully guards its doors and gates. But tell me, how does one protect life? Have you not seen what Layman Pang said: 'To protect life, one must kill;
only when all are killed does one dwell in peace'? If you can understand the meaning within these words, [then you have it]. Iron [Staff].
The boat floats upon the water. Master Guoqing Daowu said: "Dharma after dharma is the dharma of non-arising; mind after mind is the mind of quiescent extinction.
This is the place where the thousand sages share the same source. At midday, they strike the watch of three. "Assembly, simply dwell in such a manner for now. Take care!"

Addressing the assembly, he raised an example: One day, while Guishan was sitting in the Dharma Hall, the storekeeper struck the wooden fish, and the fire-head threw down his fire-fork and clapped his hands, laughing loudly.
Guishan said, "There is such a person among the assembly," and he called him over to question him.
"What do you say to this? The Fire-Head monk said, "I did not eat my gruel and was hungry; that is why I am joyful. Guishan then nodded his head.
Later, Jingqing said, "It is clear that there was no one in Guishan’s assembly. Wulong said, "It is clear that there was someone in Guishan’s assembly.
Gusuan said, "There was someone in Guishan’s assembly; he has drawn a picture of empty space."
Regarding these eyebrows and eyes: there was no one among the assembly at Guishan who could pluck out the eyes of the Vajra-being.
But as for the head of the storehouse striking the wooden fish and the fire-head throwing the fire-tongs—what was the meaning behind Guishan’s nodding?
Three pieces of firewood, toasted in the shape of the character "品" (piǎn). There is no need to wield the brush; the literary brilliance is already revealed. Even so, what about Gushan today?
He sat upon the Dharma Hall; the great assembly crowded upward to pay their respects and stood in formation.
They listened as the old monk chattered incessantly, discussing the present and the past, speaking of yellow and white paths. "Is there someone here? Or is there no one?
If you say there is no one, why do they come at the sound of the bell? If you say there is someone, why do they come at the sound of the bell?
"The sound does not come. If it comes, who is it? If it does not come, who again is it? After a long silence, he said, "The assembly, return to the hall;
each of you should investigate this thoroughly."

Addressing the assembly, he raised the following case: When Chan Master Longxing Zongjing first visited Xuefeng to clarify the essential point of the mind, he immediately received his seal of approval.
He then vowed to serve as the head cook for over ten years to perform manual labor. One day, while bare-chested in the assembly hall, he was nailing up a curtain.
Seeing this, Xuefeng remarked, "In the future, you shall dwell in a monastery with a thousand followers; yet among them, there will not be one [who understands]."

He was a monk-disciple. He bowed respectfully to apologize for his transgressions and repent. Later, he took leave to return to Taizhou. The King of Qian invited him to reside at Longxing Monastery, where the assembly numbered over a thousand;
they were all disciples who recited and practiced the Three Schools. Indeed, it was just as Xuefeng had predicted. The Master said: "The times belong to the Dharma of the Final Age;
monasteries are declining in their later years, and the spiritual faculties of people are shallow and vulgar. To seek even one person who truly recites and practices the Three Schools is difficult."
It cannot be attained; how much less so for a patch-robed monk (*śramaṇera*)? But tell me, what ultimate excellence does a patch-robed monk possess? After a long silence, he said:
"If one does not sleep on the same bed, how can one know that the lining of the quilt is worn through?"
Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised this case: A monk asked Master Dongshan, "Ordinarily, you instruct students to practice the 'Bird Path.
What is the Bird Path? Dongshan said, "Not meeting a single person. The monk asked, "How does one travel it? Dongshan said, "One must simply proceed with no self-interest beneath one's feet.
The monk asked, "Is traveling the Bird Path not precisely one’s original face? Dongshan said, "Why do you, Reverend, [ask this]?"
To recognize a slave as a lord. [A monk] asked, "What is one's original face? Dōsan said, "Not walking the bird-path.
The Master said, "Dōsan speaking thus may be called 'striking the head of a stone man with a staff; *bò bò*, discussing the actual matter, acting intimately for others.
Nevertheless, there is yet another verse, which I cannot help but present to the assembly: 'Walking the bird-path, or not...'"
"Acting! It appears one is still traversing the path. The original face has no place to hide; even if Gu Kaizhi were to try, he could not paint it.
Addressing the assembly, the Master said: "As for this matter, although it is already manifest, the investigation, realization, and clarification thereof also depend upon [one's own effort]."
It depends upon the conditions and the timing; one cannot obtain it through restless seeking. Therefore, an ancient worthy said:
"Know that this matter exists, but simply let not a single thought cease. He further said: "Grind it with years and months; there is nothing that cannot be attained.
Thus, in the past, Xuefeng ascended Mount Touzi nine times and sought his teacher at Dongshan for definitive discernment; subsequently, he was enlightened atop San Dian on Mount Ao.
Attaining the Way: Chan Master Changqing Ling spent over twenty years coming and going at the gates of Xuefeng and Xuansha;

he sat until seven bundles of rush mats were worn through, yet it was only upon rolling up the curtain that he attained great enlightenment. Yunyan spent twenty years under Baizhang before the lamp of his mind failed to continue;
it was only after meeting Yaoshan that he finally reached full realization. These were all great spiritual masters of the past.

Having labored for such a long duration and attained the Way with such slowness, he was thus able to continue the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom, radiating its brilliance throughout antiquity and the present.
How could this compare to the people of these times who merely let words enter their ears and pass out of their mouths, busily seeking to sell themselves to others?
In the end, what matters have they actually resolved? What connection do they have to their own true nature? Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
I once used playing the lute to demonstrate the application of the mind to my students. I said that while it is certainly not possible if [the strings] are too loose, they must also not be too tight.
Only when the mind is properly tuned can one attain the Way. If one is violent toward the Way, such violence leads to physical exhaustion.

When the body is exhausted, the mind gives rise to affliction. When the mind gives rise to affliction, one's practice regresses. Once practice has regressed, retribution will surely be added. However...

"Purity, tranquility, and bliss—the Way is not lost. O Great Assembly! These four characters, "Purity, Tranquility, and Bliss," are what Śākyamuni, the Old Man, carved from his own belly, gouged from his heart, and etched into our very bones to show us.
If you can understand them and believe in them, then even if your bones were ground to powder and your body shattered to pieces, there would be no way to repay him.
If you do not know them and do not believe them, it is your own fault; how could this concern only this present life? Only...
I fear that for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, all have gone astray from this very point.
Do you understand? Take care. Addressing the assembly, he raised an ancient case: Once, when a monk came to visit Xuefeng, the Master asked, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "From Zhejiang. Xuefeng asked, "By boat or by land? The monk said, "I have not traversed either path. Xuefeng asked, "How then did you get here? The monk...
He asked, "What obstacles are there? The monk was struck and driven out. Ten years later, the monk returned. Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from?
The monk said, "From Hunan. Xuefeng asked, "How far is it from here? The monk said, "It is not separated [by anything].
Xuefeng held up his whisk and asked, "Is it not separated by this? The monk said, "If it were separated, how could I have reached this place?"
Xuefeng also struck him and drove him out. Afterward, whenever the monk encountered anyone, he would invariably curse Xuefeng.
A fellow practitioner who had heard of this went specifically to visit him and asked, "Why do you curse Xuefeng? The monk recounted the two preceding incidents.
The companion rebuked him severely and pointed out the truth to him. The monk wept bitterly; thereafter, every midnight, he would burn incense and prostrate toward the direction of Xuefeng.
[The monk] bows. The Master says: "To snatch away the food and drive away the oxen—this was the ordinary method of the old man Xuefeng.
To cast a full hand of gold right before one's face is likewise the compassionate heart that exhausts [the student]. This monk missed it twice; how could he not be scolded?
Had it not been for a fellow traveler pointing it out, even until Maitreya’s descent into the world, there would have been no end to the scolding. Nevertheless..."
It is so. Today, such a monk who knows how to revile is indeed hard to find. I dare ask the assembly:
regarding Xuefeng’s two instances of issuing commands, where did he "seize the food and drive away the plowman," and where did he "cast a handful of gold directly into his face"?
If you can discern these here, I grant that he possesses the true eye.
The Winter Retreat Opening Address for the Assembly: This morning is the fifteenth day of the tenth month; the winter-month retreat has been duly established.

Everyone has cast off body and mind. The stone head is originally a fierce tiger; with a single arrow, it pierces through to that other side. In every dharma, there is nothing at all that is obstructed.
The clay ox leaps across the sea; the wooden horse gallops up to heaven. Tell me, whose affair is this?
After a long silence, he said: "Shang Daren Qiu Yiji."
On his birthday, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "When the World-Honored One held up the flower, it was like gazing afar at mountains that possess color;
when Kāśyapa smiled, it was like listening closely to water that has no sound. I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa, which I entrust to Mahākāśyapa."
Protect and uphold this transmission and transformation so that it shall not be severed. "The falling flower has the intention to follow the flowing water;
the flowing water has no mind to cherish the falling flower. Although it is thus, how about [the occasion] when he was born from the right side beneath the Ashvattha tree?
Last night the iron ox conceived a calf; at dawn it gave birth to a white crow.

On the first day of the year, the Wuchen era, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Yesterday was the tail of the old year; today is the head of the new year. Moment by moment, there is no abiding;
time and seasons pass like a flowing stream. Yet within this, there is one person for whom time and seasons have no connection—neither new nor old."
It is not something else; it is ever-present within movement and function. Within movement and function, it cannot be covered over or concealed.
If you can truly recognize this person, it is like a child finding its mother; only then do you have the capacity for study and practice.

If it is otherwise, you will spend your years knocking about outside the gate, prying and fiddling with words and letters, making a living amidst the sense bases and objects, wandering aimlessly to the ends of the earth in bitter hardship.
Suffering! Whose fault is this? Although it is thus, tell me: how, after all, does this person come to recognize him?
After a long silence, he said: "When seen with total clarity, not a single thing exists; the verification before birth is even more distinct."
Addressing the assembly, the Master said: "Yesterday, when we entered the hall to discuss the Gate of Non-duality, it was not yet thoroughly resolved.
Today, before this great assembly, I cannot help but bring it up once more, so that everyone may truly know it. He then said:
"The entire earth is this Gate of Non-duality; all people of past and present are entirely within it, coming and going without any obstruction."

To block and obstruct. This was why, at that time during the single assembly in the city of Vaiśālī, thirty-two bodhisattvas spoke in such a manner, the Layman Vimalakīrti remained silent in such a manner, and the Great Being Mañjuśrī offered praise in such a manner.
This was to serve as a signpost for those who come later. If you do not "lift up and go" immediately, it will instead result in being left behind. Even if you were to further say:
Speaking when it is silent, and remaining silent when it is spoken; the Great Gate of Giving is opened wide without obstruction. Look closely: seeking intimacy, one instead becomes distant.
How does this compare to the present assembly, who upon hearing the bell, immediately ascend;

having performed their prostrations, they descend. Those returning to the hall go to the hall; those returning to the quarters go to the quarters. They walk straight ahead—what hindrance could there be?
Even so, you must not so much as move a single toe. To move it is to receive thirty blows of the staff.
(Five Questions for Inquiry) First Question:
Since we do not inquire about the time before one's parents were born, tell me a word regarding what happens after one has died and been cremated.
The second question: Before Śākyamuni had appeared in the world and before Bodhidharma had come from the West, who was it that upheld the Buddha-Dharma?
The third question: Setting aside the path of Chan and the Buddha-Dharma to one side, speak a single word from the ground of reality.
Question Four: What is the Buddha Without Stain?
Question Five: What is the Buddha Free from Stain?
*Record of Chan Master Gushan Weilin’s Return to the Mountain*, Volume Three.
Attendant Fáyún records this Buddhist service upon returning to the mountain to pay respects at the stupa of National Preceptor Kāṅshàng Yàn, the founder of the monastery.
An ancient master from eight hundred years ago—how many have known his path through the night? This true message is without gap between past and present;
simply look now at this very moment of direct encounter. How is this one phrase of direct encounter? He then burned incense.
I pay respects at the stupa of the late Master, my Preceptor:
this foolish child does not understand matters, and everywhere he has broadcasted the family’s disgrace. Today he suddenly returns, possessing nothing at all.
This single incense offering is burned before the stupa; the green pines and white stones remain as they were.

On the ninth anniversary of the passing of the First Patriarch Bodhidharma—who sat facing the wall for nine years—his "single phrase of settling the mind" has been passed down through error until the present day. In vain do we speak of his single shoe.
Returning West, a wind of raw stench rises throughout the world at Shaolin.
On the anniversary of Master Shouchang’s passing, Huanglong Peak and Lingshi Peak (Amlakṣika) compete for prominence; Great Mountain and Not-Great Mountain revile one another. Today—
Though timely and seasonal, they cannot avoid being listed together below: a cup of green tea and a brazier of incense—these shall serve as a topic of conversation for ten thousand ages.

It has been many years since the Master Zhenji left the mountain; wherever one goes, one encounters his "returning on the anniversary of his death. Today he has suddenly returned, and it is likewise difficult to avoid him.
O Great Assembly, the Elder Zhenji is here! The plum blossoms do not vie with the snow; facing the sun, they compete in their full splendor.
The anniversary of my late teacher, the Old Monk:
in days past he did not go when he should have gone; this morning he still does not come when he should come. Having cut off the path above, there is no noble station;
a single branch of cold plum blossoms opens amidst the snow.
Sweeping the Stupa of the Ancestor Yun Kong at Lingshan:
The ancestral stupa towers loftily above a thousand peaks; Beneath its feet, the lush greenery is entirely a fine mountain. Today I come again to sweep the withered leaves;
His compassionate countenance is half-concealed amidst the white clouds.
I have swept the stupa of my late master Wuming Shouchang for many years without sweeping it;
yet the shadow of my master’s stupa pervades the three thousand worlds. Today, I again offer this incense to manifest it:
atop the peak of Huanglong, the waves surge to the heavens.
Sweeping the Stupa of Master Lianchi of Yunqi (Two Poems) The transmission of robes and fly-whisks has spread throughout the world;
The Zen practitioners of the entire nation have gone wild. Had it not been for my father’s opening of the path of pure karma, Who would know where to seek the bridge across the stream?
In the autumn of the year Yi-mao, the grandfather was born; in the winter of the year Yi-mao, the grandson was extinguished.
Grandfather and grandson suddenly meet face-to-face, bringing forth a single snowflake from the red furnace.

Visiting Bingyao to Pay Homage at the Stupa of Master Taowen (Two Poems) Bogu Mountain, Baoshan, and Bingyao— In receiving instruction from these three places, I did not dare find the distance a burden. The Great Dharma was personally pointed out by the Elder;
Like a mosquito or gnat drinking from the sea, my gratitude is difficult to repay.
Fifty years have passed since my master entered nirvana; three times I have burned the incense of my heart before his stupa. If you ask for the essential meaning of my master’s teaching:
it lies where a thousand peaks encircle the white clouds.

Sweeping the Stupa of the Late Dharma Master Gudao (Two Poems) The Ancient Amitābha beneath the Gate of Yunqi, His merit in propagating the Western Paradise was greatest. I recall those years when I once sat among his disciples;
To this day, his dharma words still ring out clearly.
This year’s year is last year’s year; a single piece of sandalwood burns before the stupa. Do not say that life and death constitute a permanent parting;
you must know that the Way of the Teacher transcends both center and periphery.
Sweeping the Stupa of Master Xinyi Lao (Two Poems) Fifty years ago I once escorted you through hardship;
I received your instructions and was freed from all doubt. The lineages of Tiantai, Sanlun, Xing, and Xiang have been transmitted afar;
The vast rain of Dharma is known throughout the world.
Today, from afar, I hold aloft a single incense offering; upon Mount Fahua, I pay homage to the King of Emptiness.
Though it is said that Min and Zhejiang are separated by a thousand li, let us observe how the blue smoke penetrates to the Highest Realm.
Sweeping the Stupa of Master Lingyuan Lao (Two Poems) The Dharma was personally transmitted from Tuoqiao by the Prime Minister of Tai;
With a simple headcloth, he ascended the seat in carefree ease. Only in his later years did he assume the full appearance of a Bhikṣu;
His Dharma-merit was vast and expansive, like the tide of the sea.
In the Zhaokeng Hall, we personally saw you off; such auspicious signs of nirvana are rarely heard of in this world.
Now that the white stupa is buried in green grass, where can one burn the incense of the heart from a thousand miles away?
Sweeping Snow at the Pagoda of Dharma Master Sōrō (Two Poems) In years past, I sought the Way at Chūkō-ji;

for half a year we stayed together, our discussions flourishing. You frequently raised the principles of the Middle Way within form and fragrance, and the teachings and contemplations of our school were fully revealed.
The white stupa remains within Nāgārjuna’s hermitage; the Dharma-body is unharmed, having long since transcended words. With a single offering of incense, I personally present it face-to-face;
like the moon reflected in a clear pool, how could there be any trace?
On the occasion of the celebration of the one hundred and tenth year of our late teacher, the Old Monk, he held up his incense and said:
"The Master’s age is one hundred and ten; light radiates throughout the entire world. The Stone Drum roars amidst the clouds; the Clay Ox bellows from the bottom of the sea."
Neither ordinary nor holy; neither ceasing nor arising. For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the ancient tree has ever flourished.
How do you express a single phrase of special celebration for this very day? After a long silence, he said: "I have already made offerings to it;
now I come again to behold it in person."
Ten Verses on Yearning for the Past in the Zen Tradition (With Preface):
The style of Chan has already declined, and its momentum cannot be turned back. Thus, I have composed these ten verses yearning for the past, to express my reverent admiration.
Reflections. To share these with those who possess resolve:

The Master of Mount Yin in Tanzhou—this mountain has no path, so who could enter it? Suddenly, a hidden master arrived and cleared it away; facing him, the pure breeze brushes across the white clouds.
The Moon: Why need a thatched hut be moved even deeper?
Master Liang has summoned empty space to expound the sutras; when artifice is exhausted, one awakens all the more clearly. Once gone to the Western Mountain, there is no trace left behind.
Rest. For ten thousand ages the colors of the peaks turn ever greener.
Chan Master Fachang of Mount Daimei in Mingzhou once personally received the essential meaning at West River.
Deep within Mount Daimei, he skillfully concealed his person; though floating clouds shift and turn, his mind remained without [distraction].
[The text] was revised. Eating pine needles and wearing lotus leaves, his Way was not one of poverty.

Layman Pang of Xiangzhou had sons and daughters whom he did not marry off; together they traveled to various regions to discuss the essence of the Way. His wealth of a million households was entrusted to Xiang.
Water. The reputation of Lüli began from this point.

As for the Monk of the Fishing Boat guiding disciples and leading a community, that is not my business. Once you have caught that golden-scaled fish, you may simply rest. One day, the fishing boat capsized.
Afterwards, green mountains and clear waters flow on together in eternity.

When the Venerable Chen [Changsha] encountered Linji and Yunmen, he fell into their living trap; who could have known that he was hiding his body while revealing his shadow? In a quiet room at an ancient temple, he weaves reeds.
Shoes. How bitter! The lightning-flash of his spiritual edge was swift.

When Chan Master Fuyong Kai’s Way reached its zenith under Master Taiyang, he risked his life to uphold the transmission; how could he have sought fame? Rather than offend the dragon’s scales, he willingly accepted demotion.
Exiled. From this point on, Caoxi was once again clear and pure.
The venerable master Qing-su attended Ci-ming for over ten autumns; following his teacher’s final instructions, he buried his head in practice. On a narrow path at Long-an, they met.
[Signature]. At the end of the verse, the transmission brings a face full of shame.

At Shitou An’s monastery, the Tiger of Meaning turns his body; the matter is no small one. Deep within the green vines, I decline idle fame. Do not speak of the leisure of Chan, for its blessings are not...
Having attained this, one wins the right to sleep high and dream of many lifetimes.
When Master Gaofeng’s pillow fell to the ground, what was the matter? He entered the thousand peaks directly and closed his own door, making death his only deadline; do you not understand?
Beholding it: A lofty wind rises ten thousand fathoms, making all ascent and climbing impossible.
*Gushan Jijing* (Four Poems on the Scenery of Mount Gu):
Ten Thousand Pines Encircle the Temple.

Ten thousand pines float in azure, embracing the Zen grove; the home mountain of the dragon-elephants has been so from ancient times to the present. There is no need for this old monk to point it out repeatedly;
the wind and waves transmit the mind day and night.

The traces of the Water-Drinker’s departure reveal a cliff split open by heaven, as if sharing the same expanse as the Gorges of Ba; thunderous roars constantly echo within these mountains. Who would say that water is an insentient thing?
With a single roar, it turns its head, and the ten thousand sounds fall silent.

In the stillness of night, the sound of the bell—this hundred-foot whale-bell atop the perilous tower—is heard. Deeply silent at the third watch, the moonlight is fresh and new. A single distant stroke of the pestle makes the mountains and peaks tremble;
it startles the practitioner from his seated meditation with ease.
Deep in the night, the Buddha’s name was called;
this body was cast upon the meditation platform. In a dream, one gives rise to crosswise attachments; with a single call of the Buddha’s name, one is awakened.
Only then does one realize that here, the dawn has already broken.
On the day of Yi-chou in the spring, I, Xie Jian-sheng, accompanied by the scholar Guang-wen and the monk Kai-yue, entered the mountains to visit me.

Together we toured He-shui Yan (Water-drinking Rock), brewed tea from Longquan (Dragon Spring) water, ascended Feng-po (Phoenix Slope), and gazed upon the various scenic wonders while reading the remains left by former sages on the stone walls;
we could not help but feel profound reflections on the passage of time between past and present.
Master Xi-ung visited me in Mount Gu; on this day, our shared delight in wandering was the same. Upon the rocks, the ancients have all long since departed;
by the pavilion, the passing travelers still hasten by. Dragon-head springs brew fresh tea over new fires; phoenix-tail mosses tread upon ancient tracks.
Gazing far into the distance, what is there to be seen? Only the great river, day and night, vying to flow toward the east.
Zang Kuiting, Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat, entered the mountains to visit me. We engaged in an animated discussion on the Pure Land and composed this verse to reflect upon it:

Leaves falling, one is startled by the early autumn; Meeting you, we speak of the Way with lingering leisure. One might vainly suspect the Buddha’s words to be false, But one must believe that it is one's own mind that is deluded.

The Saha world (Saha means "Endurance") has finally ceased its hardships; the Land of Bliss can be expected from afar. Liu and Lei were the first at the Lotus Society (Liu Yimin and Lei Cizong entered the Lotus Society on Mount Lu).

[Yimin] took Pure Land as his primary practice. When Master Huiyuan was about to pass away, he saw Yimin attending Amitābha Buddha, who came to welcome him, saying: "You resolved your mind before I did; why have you come so late? For a thousand ages, this remains a fragrant model.
To Layman Chen Jizhi:
We have been parted for over ten years; how many changes this world has undergone! Today you suddenly return; I rejoice at beholding your face once more.

Truly, your noble spirit is like a king; your divine intelligence flashes like lightning. From this very sign, one may discern the source of longevity; you are able to turn the hours and moments yourself.
Alas, I am so utterly decrepit that not a single thing is worth envying. All day long I merely shut my door, reciting only one or two scrolls of scripture.
I hear that at sixty-five, you have arranged a grand banquet in your magnificent hall. Your guests gather like clouds, and their cries of joy shake the capital.
Hastily I compose these rustic words to pray for your long life and prosperity. As we gaze upon one another before this spread of snowy silk walls, neither of us grows weary of the other’s sight.

Long-lived Lord of the Sea, Magistrate of Haiyin State, you retired from office beneath the trees and joyfully behold me. At seventy years of age, such a rarity is seldom heard of. Your mind is like still water, reflecting the vast azure;

your countenance resembles that of an immortal, purifying all worldly dust. As peach and plum blossoms bloom in the full warmth of spring, your spirit for the misty peaks and clouds is unrestrained—this is the Way.
Amidst these pressing matters, I look afar and think of the assembly of eminent scholars gathered in the hall, together admiring the auspicious cloud-patterned calligraphy upon the Southern Mountain.
Layman Ning of Wushi has entered the mountains to fulfill his precepts, coinciding with his sixtieth birthday; I offer this verse to celebrate it.
On the first day of my sixty-first year, I personally ascended the Shigou altar. Having suddenly perfected the three aggregates of merit, how could I dread the hardships of the four great vows?
Every matter is fulfilled in Bodhi; every thought is vast within the Dharma-realm. As the Mount Shou rises ten thousand fathoms high, I rejoice to behold it together with the assembly.
Seeing off Su Zhong, a Man of Virtue, as he returns to Zhenji (Two Poems) He comes personally from the Dharma-cave of Yunqi;
The source is deep, the stream far-reaching—how profound his thoughts! The two mountain superintendents exert their full strength;
His conduct and deeds are towering, utterly free from a speck of dust.
It is now exactly the beginning of summer; with no means to turn back my heart, I linger for your sake.
Having traveled through all the hundred-fold perilous rapids, I have finally realized that my home mountain lies right above my head.

If one were to murmur with the lips, deliberating whether Chan and Pure Land are the same or different, one would find oneself surrounded on both sides by the late Master Yunqi Lianchi and the Great Patriarch Shouchang Wuming—both of whom have their own lineages of Dharma heirs—who sit in attendance, listening with respectful hands folded. To the left, one holds...
The one sitting with ease upon a low table is the Venerable Master Wuyi of Boshan.
To the right, sitting upright with hands folded in his sleeves, is my late teacher, the Elder Yongjue. Beside Boshan, standing solemnly and silent, is Chan Master Xueguan Yin.

The Inscription. Beneath the Snow Barrier, the one leaning against the rock with his head raised is the Abbot of Yimai, my preceptor, the Venerable Zhiguang.

The two figures in the distance approaching over the bridge—the one in front is the Abbot Chunyi, and the one behind holding a staff is... [the text ends].

every single element possesses a vital life-force beyond counting. Alas! The various patriarchs have passed away, and I alone remain.
After his passing, there was no means to circulate and propagate [his teachings]. That which can be transmitted is but a shadow;

that which cannot be transmitted is not the shadow. If one can, through what is transmissible, attain that which is non-transmissible, then how could it be a hollow claim that "the assembly on Vulture Peak has never truly dispersed"? Or perhaps, one remains lingering before the painted images.
To seek it within the realm of mere physical resemblance is like marking the boat after the sword has long since departed.
I cannot help but sigh deeply once more.
In the *Daśavidyā-śāstra* by the Elder Fazang, the sixth stage of the Bodhisattva, the Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*), is correlated with the position of the Pratyekabuddha.

By means of ten gates, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination in both direct and reverse order, thereby accomplishing the gate of Prajñā and attaining mastery over the three emptinesses, so that wisdom manifests before one. — Zhaobo Changzhe.
Having already explained this in the treatise, I further clarify its essential meaning through ten points, calling it the *Daśavidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Ten Clarifications).

Its purport is that the twelvefold dependent origination is both the great ocean of suffering in which all sentient beings pursue delusion and lose sight of the truth, circling incessantly upon the waves of birth and death; and it is also the Great City of Jewel Adornment belonging to all Buddhas.

This is also the Flower Forest Garden where Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra constantly dwell and reside; they perpetually manifest their physical bodies before all assemblies of sentient beings to teach and transform them without ceasing.

Because delusion regarding the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) is termed "all sentient beings," and awakening to these twelve links as being the Buddha, it follows that both sentient beings and the links of existence are devoid of self-nature.

By nature, the secondary afflictions—ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases—correspond with one another to produce contact, sensation, craving, grasping, and becoming, thereby forming the body of the five aggregates;

thus, there is the constant circulation of birth, aging, and death. If, however, one uses the power of skillful means through the contemplation of morality, concentration, and wisdom to illuminate the essential nature and characteristics of one’s own body and mind, they are all empty of intrinsic nature, with nothing existing internally or externally; this is precisely what sentient beings [are].

The mind is the entirety of the ocean of Buddha-wisdom. Furthermore, by nurturing great kindness and great compassion through the wisdom of emptiness, one enters the ocean of birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings, like a lotus flower dwelling in water without being defiled.

If one were to weary of the twelve links of dependent origination and seek liberation elsewhere, it would be like abandoning ice while seeking water, or chasing a mirage in search of a drink. If one illuminates [reality] with the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, [one realizes this].

When both mind and objects are entirely extinguished, the sun of wisdom naturally becomes clear and bright. It is like a treasure trove within the house of a poor woman, manifesting spontaneously without being sought;
or like the pearl within the garment of a destitute son, appearing naturally without effort. This is the essential purport of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s sudden and perfect teaching.
Master Li specifically extracted and pointed this out to people; it is most direct and vital. Its kindness is so great that it is difficult to repay. [End of] Wall Inscription.
A person from Jiuchuan contributed funds to carve the printing blocks so that they might be widely circulated. Might this not be one who has gained insight herein and knows how to repay kindness?
Postscript on the Carving of the Record of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s Attainment of Enlightenment.

In the past, I read the "Preface to Tengwang Pavilion" composed by Prince Wenxuan during his youth. His celestial inspiration was uniquely inspired, and he possessed both talent and learning in abundance.
Although it was merely a brush-stroke performed on the spot for guests, it remains a peerless masterpiece for all eternity;
even a veteran scholar of vast learning and grand rhetoric could not surpass it. Later, I also read the "Record of the Enlightenment of Śākyamuni Tathāgata" which he compiled.
Although it is fundamentally based on the *Śākyaputra-vamśa*, it is structured through four-character and six-character prosody; every sentence expresses his own insight.
Even veteran Chan masters who have deeply penetrated the innermost recesses of the Buddha-dharma could hardly surpass this.
It is evident that the Prajñā-pāramitā has its own origins here. Truly an inconceivable person! Now, observing this record written by Grand Historian Dong, it is...
In accordance with the command of the Venerable Elder Zibo, this work was completed after two cycles of twelve years. It is truly worthy of being called a supreme treasure of the Dharma.

May readers contemplate its calligraphy and comprehend its literary intent, thereby gaining a clear vision of the Tathāgata’s deeds during his single lifetime in descending to benefit sentient beings.
By planting the seeds of bodhi and creating the causes for Buddhahood, its benefit to the world is truly inconceivable.
The virtuous man, San-shan Lin Zi, was a man of broad learning who cherished antiquity. His family preserved this epistle, which he brought forth to show me; I marveled deeply at its rarity.
He then sought a skilled artisan to engrave a copy so as to propagate its transmission—this, surely, was the very heart of Master Lin’s intention.

Beyond his mastery of literary composition, Mr. Gao Siyi indulges in the playful art of calligraphy and painting; his renown in these fields was already established by the age of twenty.

This year I am thirty-six years of age. Having recently recovered from an illness, I took up my brush and produced several scrolls of running and cursive script, which I have sent for your inspection.
My fellow monk Jiwang and I examined them closely for many days, unable to bear putting them down;

we marveled deeply at how his innate talent and calligraphic power far transcend the ordinary and cannot be rivaled. Among these, the single scroll he transcribed of the "Fu on the Imperial Horse" is particularly refined.

The radiance it emits when viewed by people is particularly extraordinary and peerless. Not only do its physical forms, strokes, initial brushstrokes, and structural compositions leave nothing that does not resemble the original, but it also captures its entire spirit.
Even if Lümen were to rise again, he would likely be unable to distinguish whether this was his own work or a copy made by another;
such is the extent to which its refined meaning has entered the realm of the divine. It truly ought to be carved upon stone.
Through this transmission, he shall gallop side by side with the masters Su, Huang, Mi, and Cai throughout the expanse of heaven and earth.

This concludes the Record of the Beisi Hall.
Zhiceng occupies the upper reaches of the Eight Min regions; its mountains are vermilion and its waters are azure, its customs are profound and its people simple.

Former sages were born therein, many of whom studied the Odes, the Documents, the Rites, and righteousness. Furthermore, they have long held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem, understanding the doctrines of cause and effect, sin and merit, as well as loyalty, filial piety, integrity, and heroism—principles that shine brightly throughout the historical records for over a thousand years since the census registers of Emperor Wu of the Han.
Although the patterns of order and chaos have varied throughout antiquity and the present, this city has remained free from calamity.
During the Five Dynasties period, Wang Yanzheng usurped the title of king in Jianzhou, prompting the Southern Tang to dispatch Cha Wenhui with an army to attack him.

With Bian Hao and Wang Jianfeng serving as generals, they plotted to massacre the city. Lady Lian, the wife of Chancellor Zhang Zijing, protected it. During the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, Fan...
For seven years, you have usurped and occupied the three prefectures of Yan, Jian, and Shao.

You were defeated by the Great General Han Shizhong, yet you were protected and preserved by Prime Minister Li Gonggang; thus, your name remains as if alive within the ancestral rites for a thousand years.

Now that the Imperial Qing has established its capital, in the eighth month of the third year of the Shunzhi era (the Bingxu year), the great army entered Fujian. The four classes of the people turned toward the transformation, and even the chickens and dogs...
There was no alarm; the districts, counties, cities, and towns remained as peaceful and settled as before.

On the fourth day of the seventh month of the following year, the *dinghai* year, a man named Wang Qi—of unknown provincial origin—was secretly residing in Min. He plotted treason and coerced the Prince of Yuxi to rise up from Zigutian.
Leading several thousand rebel subjects, he seized and occupied the city, unleashing false executions and plundering. The various districts were thrown into turmoil. Troops...
The Circuit Intendant Gu fled to Fuzhou with his family. The Prefect Gao died defending the city. Many soldiers were killed in battle.
The local gentry and commoners were forbidden from leaving, suffering incessant torment; the people had no means to appeal their grievances. Eight months passed.
The armies of Zhejiang and Jiangsu attacked repeatedly but could not take it. In the second month of the following year, Wuzi, an imperial edict was issued by the Five Ministries.
The Hall Commandant led over one hundred thousand troops to besiege the gates from all eight sides. Deep pits were dug in circles outside the city walls;
even flying kites could not cross them, and not a single person escaped. Cannons thundered across the earth and arrows fell like rain.
For more than forty days, there was never a moment’s respite. Among them, the wounded and dead were beyond counting. At that time, there was no such thing as disciplined training.
The person who was Lord Li, the Chancellor, rose to rescue them; yet they were like chickens in a cage or fish in a cauldron, sitting and waiting for their own destruction.
How tragic this is! On the fourth day of the fourth month, the city fell. Fires broke out on all sides and soldiers rose up like swarms of bees, filling the city.
They vied with one another in slaughter; men, women, the old, and the young had their bodies shattered amidst the blades and arrows, their bones pierced through.
Within the arrowheads, there were those who had conspired with their neighbors to set fire to their homes and burn their entire families alive;
those who had taken their wives and children by the hand and leaped together into ponds or wells; those who had led their kinsmen to close their doors and hang themselves;

those whose young children and young wives were separated from them for life or death as they were plundered away; and furthermore, those righteous men and chaste women who maintained their integrity unto death.
Those who turn back to face white blades and do not shrink from fire or water encounter a fierce conflagration that stretches across the heavens for seven days and nights without ceasing.
Jade and stone are incinerated until nothing remains; corpses pile up like mountains and blood flows in rivers.

Regardless of whether they be commoners or rebels, noble or base, parents, brothers, kinsmen, relatives by marriage, friends, or acquaintances—all are equally cooked and roasted by the karma of their own slaughter.

Within a single retribution, dream-like states pursue one another as they undergo the suffering of deluded acceptance that cannot be endured. Those with merit have already transcended to the happy realms;
those with transgressions are bound once more to the gates of the underworld. As the years and months stretch on for eternity, when can one expect to emerge from this suffering?

Alas! How painful it is! Countless living beings have all become victims beneath the blade. For those with hearts of compassion, who will pity these ghosts who have no refuge? O souls of the netherworld!
Vast and profound, the lingering spirits drift aimlessly, unable to behold the Heaven of Radiance; how could they reach the path of returning to the Truth?

Only our Great Being, Avalokiteśvara, possesses compassion that shares in the same essence and gives rise to unconditional kindness. With a thousand hands he reaches out to guide us, and with a thousand eyes he perceives us clearly.

He makes no distinction between enemies and kin, delivering all equally and universally. For this reason, we have respectfully gathered various resources and selected a vast, pure site amidst the white clouds.

He constructed a hall with an inscription reading "Pensive Sorrow" (*Pei-si*). Within it were enshrined sacred images of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, along with Kṣitigarbha and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

In the side chambers, he arranged the spirit tablets of all those from the city who had perished—officials, generals, soldiers, scholars, commoners, monks, Daoists, the virtuous, as well as farmers, merchants, artisans, and laborers. Day and night, incense was burned...
Chanting the names of Buddhas from the *Dīpa-vaṃśa Sūtra* during the spring and autumn sacrifices, and offering prayers for liberation on the Zhongyuan festival,

we hope to receive the radiant grace of the Triple Gem and forever emerge from the extreme sufferings of the nine dark realms. Moreover, when filial sons and virtuous grandsons reflect upon their ancestors’ misfortunes,

and benevolent men and elders grieve for the souls of the wronged who remain submerged in oblivion, they establish great ferries and bridges to provide spiritual sustenance for both the living and the deceased, so that all may ascend together to the realm of benevolence and longevity.
May we together ascend the field of liberation. May its blessings cover the entire city, and its merit flow through eternal ages; this is my humble aspiration.
Furthermore, I have heard the lament for ancient battlefields: "Who has no parents? They carried us in their arms and bore us upon their backs, fearing we might not live long.
Who has no brothers? They were like one’s feet and hands. Who has no wife? She was like a guest or a friend. What kindness did they show in giving life, that we should take it away?"
"What fault is there? Is it not true that this city of Wuzhi (Wucheng) is now a battlefield?

Throughout the entire city, fathers, mothers, brothers, and wives—all without sin—are being led to their deaths. This is what is meant by 'Heaven and Earth grieve; plants and trees are struck with sorrow.

When offerings of condolence and sacrifice do not reach them, upon what shall their spirits and souls rely? Every time I reflect on this, my tears never fail to moisten my breast. In the blink of an eye, the four [directions]..."

Ten years have passed. Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not examine the truth. If I do not record this now, it will later be lost to hearing, and these various spirits will never have a day of emerging from suffering.
Therefore, I have named the hall "Sorrowful Reflection" (Beisi) and briefly recounted its origins and conclusion.
I shall engrave this upon stone to inform all future visitors as a record.
Record of the Spring at Keiryūin in Shaburi Named after Kōkō:
That the spring is named after Master Kōkō is intended to commemorate his virtue. For the Way is propagated by men, and principle is verified through events; this is no mere coincidence.
In the past, when Master Kōkō first opened up this mountain, the community was numerous yet water was scarce, making the labor of drawing and carrying it exceedingly difficult. One day...

He practiced walking meditation (caṅkrama) among the dry fields to the right of the temple. Thereupon, he struck the ground with his staff, and the spring gushed forth, bubbling up along with the staff;
the more he struck, the more it surged. He then ordered a craftsman to excavate a well to contain the water. It was about one *zhang* in depth and breadth, and its color was like milk.

Its sweetness was like that of molasses; it flowed abundantly outward, and by means of bamboo conduits, it was led back to the Cloud Kitchen (the monastery) to provide for several hundred people, never failing in either winter or summer.
This master was truly an inconceivable person. More than ten years have passed since his passing.
In the second month of the spring of the Jiazi year of the Kangxi era, I visited the mountain to pay respects at his stupa. Beholding this auspicious marvel, I marveled at its rarity.

He then named it Jinggong Spring (the Spring of Master Jing) and carved this inscription upon a stone, so that future inhabitants dwelling here might drink the water while knowing its source and not remain ignorant of its origin. Thus it is said.

Record of the Reconstruction of the Three Pagodas at Lingshi Temple Lingshi is an ancient monastery of Yurong, founded by the Tang dynasty monk Jushi (Zhizhe). Successive patriarchs of the Chan lineage have held the seat for over fifty generations.
Since the arrival of the Ming dynasty, more than three hundred years have passed; the ancestral lamp has long been extinguished, and the flame of the Buddha has grown dim. The site lies desolate...
It was rare indeed that it did not become overgrown with wild smoke and creeping weeds. Its restoration began during the Wanli era.
My elder brother, the senior monk Cao Yuan, succeeded [to the lineage]. After Master Yuan passed away, his disciples Jiying and others were all able to embody their teacher’s intent;
internally they applied themselves to Chan and the precepts, while externally they maintained the strictness of the monastic precincts. Years passed, and they underwent many hardships.

In perilous times, through the resonance of his utmost sincerity, the fourfold assembly turned their hearts toward him. He undertook the construction of a great hall, a Dharma hall, a Hall of Heavenly Kings, two long corridors, and two pavilions for the bell and drum;
furthermore, images, the Tripitaka, as well as mountains, forests, fields, and lands were all provided in full.
Although he could not restore everything to its former state, he has already achieved seven or eight tenths of it. The monastic community numbers several hundred, [rising] at dawn...
From evening until dawn, he practiced with such unremitting diligence that the ancestral monastery, which had stood for a thousand years, was restored to its former splendor.

Is this not indeed a great event for the Dharma? Yet, the spirit towers of the successive patriarchs and the assembly of the ocean-like multitude still lay neglected among the wild weeds, and there has been no leisure to repair them.
The Chief Administrator Jizhe then consulted with the members of the Dharma family; each contributed their own possessions to jointly support this magnificent undertaking.

Furthermore, following the established model of the three stupas found in various regions, the central [stupa] enshrines the [remains of] the successive...

As for those residing in various places, all are gathered and enshrined here. The front of the altar is called the Vajradhvaja; on the left are installed the venerable elders of long standing, and on the right are concealed the diligent veterans.
Construction began on the sixteenth day of the second month of the year Kāngxī Yichou (1705) and was completed on the full moon of the second month the following year.
The Elder Ying sent a letter requesting my words to be engraved upon stone, so as to illuminate future generations.
I reflect that within this Sahā world, all conditioned phenomena change in an instant; how could their formation and destruction ever be permanent? Should a worthy person be found, it shall flourish;
should such a person not be found, it shall fall into ruin. If only the true lamp of the Triple Gem may be kept from being extinguished, then even fragments of stone from this stupa may endure.
I merely hope that future worthies will let their aspirations remain undiminished, succeeding one another in an unbroken lineage so as not to let the legacy of our predecessors fall into oblivion.

He then marveled that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm, manifesting everywhere in an inconceivable manner, such that there are no sentient beings with the necessary conditions who do not [partake of its benefits].

The Stūpa. Untroubled by any calamities, it shall eternally abide upon this mountain as a field of merit for humans and devas. The Buddha’s vows are inexhaustible; my vows are inexhaustible.

Record of the Portraits of the Patriarchs of Gushan:
I have often observed that Buddhas, patriarchs, and sentient beings all manifest directly from the Dharmakāya; they are all, in essence, shadows.

Furthermore, those who employ brush and ink create shadows upon these shadows. Although these manifestations are successively empty and still, ultimately, while the true source has no shadow, it is through shadow that it is revealed.
Not departing from reality, the Dharma-body alone is taken as the definitive standard; it is simply for the wise to be able to observe this deeply within themselves.

These have long since been carved into woodblocks and circulated throughout the monastic communities. As for...

Treating them as if I had acquired the most precious jewels, I purchased them back at a high price. Once they were mounted and framed, I enshrined them in the Zhengfazang Hall;
however, as there were various omissions and inconsistencies among them, with some preceding and succeeding one another in a disjointed manner, I privately desired to slightly...

I have compiled the five schools of the Chan tradition along with the sage-patriarchs who manifested their teachings in India and China, as well as several representative patriarchs from the Tiantai, Xianshou, Ci'en, Lotus, and Vinaya schools, so that there may be a clear framework for veneration.
At that time, due to construction work, I had no leisure to attend to this matter; thus it was delayed until the summer of the Wuchen year, a total of two [years].
In the seventeenth year [of my studies], I was finally able to commission a copyist to produce portraits from life.

These were added to the existing images of my late master and various patriarchs, totaling forty-seven new figures, bringing the total to one hundred and twenty-seven. These were bound into three scrolls within a single volume.
I then incense-burned and prostrated before each figure, inscribing the original eulogies of my late master before them. Among these, there are several figures who...
Regarding that which my former teacher had not yet ascended, I have presumptuously supplemented it with eulogies. At this time, I am already seventy-four years old;
reflecting on this, I consider how life passes swiftly without lingering for even a moment. It is fortunate that Heaven has granted me these years so that I may bring this great matter to completion.
Is this not because I possessed a subtle affinity for *prajñā* from long ago? Thus, in this autumn of the decline of the Dharma-ending age, I have brought it to fulfillment.
Is this not a supreme merit? Alas! Though the patriarchs have passed away, their countenances appear as if they were still alive.
If a wise person can see their true form through their shadow, and seeing their form, perceive their mind, then those patriarchs are neither before nor after us;
one is then personally relying at their feet, personally hearing their sighs and laughter, and personally receiving their staff and shouts. How could this be a matter of past and present?

Can time and place create a separation? If one merely lingers in play with the image or speculates upon the words and phrases, they belong to the class of those who discard gold while carrying hemp; how could such a person be deemed noble?
Therefore, I have detailed its origins and conclusion so that future observers may know its provenance and understand the intent behind its contemplation. This is the portrait of the Patriarch.
