A Record of the Reconstruction of the Ancient Pūtóng Stūpa:

Formerly, when the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang first established this monastic community (*saṅghārāma*), practitioners from the ten directions gathered there to dwell together in the Dharma. All...
They ate together in the hall and sat upon the same mats, mutually exhorting one another to strive for the realization of wisdom.

When their karmic conditions were exhausted, they carried firewood to cremate the deceased; then, gathering the remaining ashes, they returned them together to the stupa. This was to manifest that the Dharma is their kin.
The principle of not forgetting those who have passed away has been followed by all the monastic communities throughout the land since the Tang dynasty;
such structures are known as "Universal Stupas" (Pútóngtǎ). The Universal Stupa at Mount Gū is situated below Bówú Peak, facing the Dual River and surrounded by ten thousand mountain ranges;

it is renowned for its magnificent scenery. Furthermore, the sand and water encircle it, and its foundation and structure are vast and spacious, making it a fitting place for seasonal offerings and ancestral rites.
It can accommodate several thousand fingers. It was established in the third year of the Daguan era of the Song dynasty.
The nineteenth-generation abbot, Chan Master Youxu, divided it into three tombs; he enshrined the remains of the assembly on the left and right, leaving the center vacant to await future abbots.
Not long after, Master Xu moved his residence to Xuefeng, where he eventually passed away. Subsequently, the twentieth-generation successor of Master Xu...
The second-generation master, Chan Master Bangjing, would always hold a wooden snake whenever he ascended the seat. People of the time called him "Wooden Snake" Monk.

After residing as abbot for many years, one day at high noon, he gathered the assembly for the Dharma hall discourse; his profound mechanism was like a roll of thunder, and he passed away while descending from the seat.
He was cremated, and his remains were placed in a small earthenware coffin and enshrined within a stone niche in the upper section of the central crypt.
After the period of [Master] Jing, those who served as abbots each built stupas, yet none surpassed this one. Nevertheless, the stupa shared the same fortunes and misfortunes as the temple;
it had remained in a state of ruin for many years. In the *dingmao* year of the Tianqi era, Chan Master Wuyi of Boshan reopened the Dharma at this mountain.
The monastic regulations were partially restored; however, it was not until the *gengwu* year of the Chongzhen era that the Monastery Superintendent began quarrying stone for repairs.
He opened the crypt, moved all the ancient remains and stones to the left side, leaving the right side empty to await future generations.

This was done so that the stone niche outside the central crypt would remain vacant. From the *jiashu* year, our late teacher, the Venerable Yongjue, entered the mountain, and all neglected affairs were fully restored.
However, this stupa had not yet been completed when more than fifty years had passed; the assembly of monks gathered like clouds, and the right crypt was filled.

On the twentieth day of the eighth month of the Wuchen year of the Daqing Kangxi era, the supervising monk Bhikṣu Fayan generously donated his robes and bowl and reopened the stupa for reconstruction.
He then moved the skeletal remains from the two side chambers back into the central one.
The left burial chamber was entirely empty, while only one-tenth remained in the right chamber; thus, those who came later could enter both the left and the right.
Once the burial was completed, they constructed stone pedestals over a foot high, covering all three chambers so that the stupa body stood majestically upon them.
These were firm, solid, and free from the danger of rainwater seeping in; furthermore, they constructed a surrounding enclosure for the stupa.
A second enclosure was added to shield it from the waters and mountains; upon reaching this stage, the construction of the stupa was largely complete.

This ensured that those living together would have a place of reliance while alive and a place of return when dead, so that the intention behind the ancient masters' establishment of monastic communities (saṃghārāma) was nearly fully realized.
Nevertheless, one must know that the true body is signless and the true stupa is seamless. Such a stupa enshrines such a body, filling the entire dharma-realm without any deficiency or excess.
Since it is free from the transitions of the four marks, how could it be subject to the calamities of the three disasters?
This is the true place of enjoyment for us to cast off our bodies and relinquish our lives.
To observe how people in this world make their living out of skulls, yet seek a mere span of earth to plan for a thousand or ten thousand years—is this not delusion?

Upon the completion of the work, I have recorded the date and time. Having fully expressed the facts, I have further developed the principle in this manner; yet, the principle is not external to the facts.
The phenomenon resides within the principle. Dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows are ultimately unobtainable; this can only be deeply observed by the wise.
This serves as the record. Record of the Re-establishment of the Baiyun Monastery.
Baiyun Xiyuan is a branch monastery of Yongquan Chan Temple on Baiyun Peak at Mount Gu.
Mount Gu was first established in the fourth year of the Jianzhong era of the Tang Dynasty, when Minister Pei Zhou invited Master Lingqiao to recite the Avatamsaka Sūtra.
He pacified the calamity of the venomous dragon that was destroying the people’s crops. A memorial was submitted to establish Huayan Monastery, which remained so for many years.
Later, it encountered the misfortune of the Huichang era; the monks fled and hid, and the site fell into overgrowth for seventy years.

Then, in the second year of the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty during the Five Dynasties period, the Bodhisattva King Wang, whose name was Shenzhi, arrived in accordance with his vows and caused the Dharma to flourish once more.

The Three Jewels were established wherever they were present. He then expended over four hundred thousand taels of silver to reopen this mountain, excavating foundations, quarrying stone, selecting timber, and recruiting craftsmen to construct a great temple complex. Its towering and magnificent splendor illuminated the crags and valleys.

He invited National Preceptor Shenyanyan to establish his monastic residence (zhuoxi) there, where he extensively propagated the fundamental tenets of the school; the assembly regularly numbered in the tens of thousands.

Furthermore, at the foot of the mountain, he separately constructed this monastery, taking the name of Baiyun Peak as its title, and designated the Baiyun Hermitage as a place for cultivation and receiving guests.
The two monasteries, upper and lower, were like a body and its arms, functioning in mutual dependence and being indispensable to one another. From that time on...
It has existed for eight hundred years, with more than eighty successive generations of masters of the Dharma presiding over it.

These details are fully recorded in the *Chuandeng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) and the *Ben-shan Liezu Lianfang Ji* (Collection of the Successive Fragrance of the Patriarchs of the Mountain). Among these, the history of its construction, modifications, and changes cannot be recounted in full.

In the *Xin-hai* year of the Hongzhi era of the Ming dynasty, the lower monastery was destroyed by fire. Chen Gongdao, the Imperial Commissioner stationed there, donated his stipend to rebuild it. During the Jiajing...
In the year Renyin, the Upper Temple was again struck by disaster, and the monastic community returned entirely to the Lower Courtyard.

Like bees in their hives or ants in their nests, each person established their own household, and the institution gradually fell into decline. In the spring of the Jiaxu year of the Chongzhen era, my late teacher, the Venerable Yongjue, came to preside over this mountain.
At that time, the former monks of the Lower Courtyard were few and far between, and being burdened by corvée labor, they had not even reached ten years before they had almost all perished.

The temple was subsequently abandoned. An invitation was then made to the Venerable Tōzan Tei to serve as its abbot; however, after several subsequent changes of leadership, none were able to restore it to prosperity.
The golden image was covered in dust, thorns and brambles filled the view, and the crumbling walls and dilapidated buildings left passersby fearing they might collapse at any moment.
Finally, the monk Weijia remained to diligently maintain the incense and lamps, but one night he died suddenly, leaving the monastery increasingly without a master.
In the Dingyou year of the Shunzhi era, my late teacher passed away, and I, by misfortune, took charge of the mountain gate.
Thereupon, the Dharma-protector Fang Guangyan led a group of local gentry and lay devotees, including Zhang Zaohui, who earnestly requested the restoration of the temple along with Shangsi Temple.
The two were unified, and the temple returned to its former splendor. I could not decline and accepted with diligent resolve. This was the summer of the Wuxu year of the Daqing reign (1658).
The following year, in the Jihai year (1659), the monastery supervisor Daowu Chengyuan recruited the assembly to seek large timbers from the Jian River.
All that was dilapidated and decayed was demolished, and the site was newly constructed: a triple gate was built in front, the Pumen Hall in the center, and [the main hall] at the rear.

The Daxiong Hall. Behind the hall is the Chaiqiu Hall, where the monastic community resides. To the right of the Pumen Hall, the Great Granary (Dacangchang) remains as it was, having been merely slightly renovated.
The golden images were reinstalled, and the fruit trees of the Southern and Northern Gardens were redeemed.
Furthermore, the Grand Governor (Dafangbo), Lord He, constructed a hall within the Southern Garden to enshrine the Great Being Samantabhadra. At that time—

The monastic community of the two temples numbered over five hundred; they possessed no ancestral lands beyond a few *sheng* and *he* of grain, possessing only several hundred *mu* of tenant-farmer fields.
Among the *bhikṣus*, there were those who practiced asceticism, vowing to labor with all their might so that, after paying the rents, the surplus could be used to support the assembly.
Should this prove insufficient, they would supplement it by means of alms-rounds. Before the three gates, a clear stream meanders like a sash. Ancient...
The banyan trees cast a dense shade. Crossing the stone bridge and turning right toward the west for several dozen paces, one reaches Tongxiao Pavilion (Pavilion of Penetrating the Heavens).
This was the very first entrance to Gushan. To the left of the triple gate, one passes Dongji Bridge and ascends along the ridge; this is known as the Tongxiao Road.
It extends for approximately ten *li*, where ancient pines screen the path and stone steps wind upward. Having collapsed and subsided over the years, they have been newly paved.
The brick-paved road leads directly to the temple; five pavilions have been constructed along the way for the convenience of resting.

Having reached this point, the general layout is complete and ancient sites have been partially restored. Consequently, one reflects that this mountain was first opened during the Tang dynasty’s Daxing era.

From the Liang, Tang, Jin, Han, through to the Song and Yuan dynasties, those who presided over the seat were all "dragons and elephants" of the Dharma, whose spiritual influence was powerfully revitalized, making it a preeminent center for the southeastern region.

This great Dharma cave entered a period of decline during the Ming dynasty; by the time of the Jiajing era and thereafter, it had fallen into extreme ruin. The cycles of fullness and emptiness, waxing and waning, are the constant laws of nature.
Over more than twenty years, my late master restored the Yongquan Monastery, reviving all that had been neglected, yet he did not have the leisure to attend to this particular temple.
I have undertaken this task with my meager strength; though I cannot hope to match every detail of its ancient precedents, I strive to fulfill my duty.

I hope that on these late autumn days at the ancestral temple, you will rekindle the dimming lamp of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and open the right path for humans and devas, guiding the fourfold assembly to return together to the ground of enlightenment.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Buddha-mind has nothing else; perfect awakening awakens the world.
Is this not precisely what is meant? I pray that my descendants will exert themselves together, examining their conduct through the precepts and clarifying...
With a mind guided by wisdom, he cultivated practice in accordance with the nature of reality and established deeds of non-action.

Looking up to the tracks left by his predecessors, he exerted his heart to reach their level, hoping not to disgrace his status as a disciple of the Buddha. This monastery was re-established from the year Jiahai; thirty years have passed since then.
The assembly of monks gathered like clouds; their usual number was eight hundred. They practiced asceticism outwardly and were diligent in meditation and precepts inwardly.
Travelers came and went in great numbers, and they received them without weariness. This was truly a transformation city [of the Dharma] from a gushing spring;

it must not fail to be recorded in its entirety so that future generations may know it. Thus I record this on the first day of the twelfth month of the Wuchen year of the Kangxi era, by one who dwells upon the mountain.
Regarding the "Traces of a Wandering Sojourn":
The Wayfarer Tripo had resided in the mountains for a long time. Various practitioners frequently questioned him regarding his origins and his spiritual journey.
He reflected that the illusory traces of a single lifetime were insufficient to instruct others; thus, though he had remained there for over thirty years, he had never brought them forth.
Recently, the Elder Qiyao and his disciples from the Southern Mountains of Fucha requested [this work] with such earnestness that I could not decline.
Thus, I have briefly set forth this general outline. My name is Dao-pai, as designated by my late teacher;
my courtesy name is Weilun, bestowed by the venerable Old Man Wengu. My self-designation is Lubo, also known as Feijia-sou. My native place is Jianning.
The Ding family of Jian’an had served the Buddha for generations. Her father, Lord Shaoxuan, was by nature a man of chivalry yet possessed a profound sense of hidden virtue.
Her mother, Zhu, served the Buddha with great devotion. At the age of thirty, she had no children; she prayed to Avalokiteśvara and subsequently conceived.
A monk who passed by her door said to her mother, "The one you are carrying is a son of the Buddha, not merely your own son. The mother replied joyfully, "If..."
She gave birth to a son. [The mother] thought, "I must have him serve the Buddha. As her time drew near and the fetus began to stir within her womb, the mother’s suffering became unbearable.
She then secretly made this vow: "Child, do not move! Child, do not move! Thereupon, it became still. After a while, it moved again; she vowed once more, and it became still as before.
The mother said joyfully, "This is my filial and obedient son. Thus he was born. It was the year Wanyili Bimao (1575).
On the second day of the eleventh month at the hour of the Rabbit (卯), he entered the schoolhouse at the age of seven to study. He was taught the *Lunyu* (Analects);

he recited it fluently and understood its general meaning with some proficiency, immediately offering explanations to others. The people regarded this as extraordinary. His father said with joy, "This son shall be the one who brings greatness to our family.
At the age of fourteen, before he had finished lecturing on the first part of the *Mencius*, he fell ill and nearly died; his mother was filled with terror day and night.
Terrified, he prayed to Avalokiteśvara, saying, "This child is originally a son of the Buddha, not my own son. Once his illness has healed, I shall cause him to serve the Buddha.

Subsequently, the illness was indeed cured. He then sent the boy forth to leave the household life. His father objected to this, but his mother said, "This child is no ordinary being of the mundane dust."

"I have already given my word to the Buddha long ago; why should you obstruct me? His father could not dissuade him, so he was sent back to Baiyun Monastery east of the commandery, where he served the elder monk Shen as his attendant for driving away crows.
The following year, he shaved his head. Regarding all the various scriptural studies, he did not rely on the instructions of a teacher;
he recited them like a flowing stream. One day, seeing a monk in the neighboring room die, he suddenly realized the impermanence of his own body.
He thus developed a profound weariness with the fiery pit of saṃsāra and became filled with indignation, resolving to transcend the mundane world.

Upon reaching the age of eighteen, he heard that the Elder Gu had come from Chu to Min and was residing at Baoshan on Mount Fenchang. Hearing this, he was filled with joy and exclaimed, "An ancient Buddha still remains!
He immediately took leave of his teacher and departed, carrying only a single bowl and a single robe, drifting away to inquire about the path to liberation from birth and death.
The elder taught him the doctrine that through the practice of *nien-fo* one will ultimately attain Buddhahood; he consequently believed it with deep conviction and without doubt.
One day, while attending the elder on a mountain walk, the elder suddenly turned back and gazed at him intently, saying, "Alas! You are a disciple capable of being taught.

It is a pity that I am too old to bring you to full realization. To the east of this stream lies Mount He; there resides the Master Yongjue, a true and virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). You—"
If one can devote one’s heart and mind to this, one will surely attain something. I had already heard the name of the Old Monk;
now, having received his instruction, it perfectly accords with my long-held aspiration. Tomorrow I was to pack my bags and depart, when the Old Monk arrived just then.
The Elder subsequently entrusted me to him. The Old Monk gave his assent and ordered that I be reported to his attendants, instructing them to have me look at the cypress tree.
As for the circumstances of the disciple: drawing water and carrying firewood, he never dared to be negligent. In the spring of the Jiaxu year of the Chongzhen era, the Old Master appeared at Gushan.
The disciple attended him from that time on, yet for four years, front and back, he found no entry into the Dharma. One day, he lamented to himself, saying:
"I have spent several years diligently practicing Chan meditation, yet I have attained no realization; furthermore, my secular studies have fallen into ruin.
Might I not be failing this life? Thinking thus, he took his leave of the Old Monk and departed from the mountain range for Hangzhou.

There, he visited various lecture halls for five years, studying the essential principles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Śūraṅgama*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Mahābodhisaṃvṛtti*, *Buddhatāśāstra*, *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, as well as the major tenets of the Tiantai and Huayan schools regarding nature and characteristics.
There was nothing he did not penetrate. Upon hearing that the Elder had passed away, the Old Monk came to Zhenji to pay his respects.
I went immediately to see him, intending to inform him that I had been listening to his lectures on the meaning of the scriptures for several years.
Suddenly, the Old Monk asked, "What about the story of the cypress tree? I was utterly bewildered and did not know how to respond. The Old Monk rebuked me, saying, "Entering the sea..."
"What limit is there to counting grains of sand? Having paid his respects and withdrawn, he was overcome with shame and remorse.

From that time on, he was restless day and night; his sleep and food lost their flavor for several months. One day, while reading the *Zhengfayan zang* (The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye), he saw Linji’s address to the assembly:
"There is a true person of no station who enters and exits through the gates of the faces of all people. Suddenly, he attained realization. Thus it was said:
[The Master] said: "So, it has always been this way, spontaneously complete. Looking back at the records of the various patriarchs, they are like splitting bamboo—nothing at all obstructed.

Furthermore, [the student] presented what he had attained through Zhenji Tong. The Old Monk questioned him, saying: 'Are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth the same as you, or are they different?
He replied: 'How could there be any difference? The Old Monk struck the desk with his ritual staff and said: 'You..."
"Why do you not feel pain? I do not know where it has fallen. The Old Monk said, "You must investigate here before you can succeed. I bowed and departed.
At that time, the Old Monk Miyun was flourishing his teachings at Tiantong. I went there to pay my respects;
upon seeing me, he immediately asked, "Are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth the same as, or different from, the student's own self? Tiantong—
He struck me immediately. I remained speechless; I bowed and withdrew. From then on, whenever I entered the room, I would simply ask in this manner and the boy would simply strike me in this manner.
I was overcome with confusion and distress. Six months passed. One day, as I was reading the sutras at the third watch, I was utterly exhausted from drowsiness.
Just as I was about to undress for sleep, suddenly the void split open and my skull shattered, and the entire body-mind manifestation appeared.
It was as if a poor man had found treasure, or as if a sick man had broken into a sweat; his exultation and joy were beyond description. He then sat upright until dawn.
The following morning, he composed a verse to present to the Abbot, saying: "Where could one water and one mountain be obtained? Every word and every silence proceeds from Him.
To be entirely right or entirely wrong is difficult to avoid or touch; Cold and warmth have always been known only by oneself. [The Master] said, "Child..."
Having finished reading it, he looked toward Xitang Chaozong and said, "It is no small matter that he has reached such a state.
He then looked toward me and asked, "What is the principle you know for yourself? I replied, "I have already presented it clearly to the Master.
Tiantong asked, "What did you present? I gave a shout. As Tiantong was about to raise his staff, I shook my sleeves and departed.
The next day, he entered the room. The attendant asked, "A fragrant breeze comes from the south; the halls and pavilions grow cool. "What is the meaning of this?
I replied with confidence, "A fragrant breeze comes from the south; the halls and pavilions grow cool.
Last night the mountains were set ablaze, leaving everyone in a flurry. The attendant said, "That is not the principle. In the past, I was once with Master [Zhaozhou]..."
Seeing that the old monk would not accept it, this led to today’s dispute. You should investigate this matter thoroughly before you can understand it.
I bowed twice and withdrew, thinking to myself: "In such an answer, what could possibly be wrong?
Furthermore, I thought I should return to Zhenji to let the Old Monk have his say once more, so I took my leave on sick leave.
His fellow practitioners then earnestly entreated him to remain, and he stayed for another month against his will. He then composed a verse to bid farewell to his companions, saying:
"Nine ascents and three climbs are called 'Elephant Bone'; Now I go or stay, how could I dare complain of hardship? The affectionate path of you gentlemen is engraved upon my heart;
Therefore, I shall meet again on the mountain at the beginning of autumn. He then departed for Zhenji to see the Old Monk. As soon as he rose from his prostrations, [the Old Monk said:]
He reported what he had realized to the Old Monk, who said with joy, "You have already entered the gate, though you have not yet ascended the hall or entered the inner chamber.
The author asked, "Is there anything further? The Old Monk replied, "You shall know this for yourself later. The author bowed and withdrew.
He remained for two months and then took his leave again, traveling to Xitianmu to visit Gaofeng’s Dead Gate for a full year. Because...
Having read Master Miaojiao Song’s *Discourse on Filial Piety*, I reflected upon my parents who had grown old. Thereupon, I descended the mountain to receive full ordination at Zhenji Temple.
After taking leave of the Elder Master, I returned to Fujian to visit my kin. Subsequently, the Elder Master also returned to Gushan.

He was able to attend upon him from time to time thereafter. Later, he built a thatched hut on Mount Dabaizhang. Being poor, he would descend the mountain every day to beg for food to provide his parents with delicacies.
When his father passed away, he subsequently ordained his mother and they entered the mountains together to cultivate the Pure Land practices for five years.
In the first month of the Gengyin year, his mother passed away. After he had grieved deeply and completed the funeral rites, he returned once more to Mount Gu.
The Old Monk said, "Go to the meditation hall. Consequently, I was appointed to the position of *vinaya-dhara* (Rector).
Whenever I entered the room for interrogation, the Old Monk overturned every previous case he had certified and refused to accept them. I was overcome with confusion and distress.
One day, the Old Monk said to me, "Do you know where the illness lies? I replied, "I do not know. The Old Monk said, "Yunmen said: 'To realize it...'"
"All dharmas are empty and hidden; it seems as though there is some thing. Is this not your own delusion?
I pondered for a long time and said, "It is precisely because of this. The Old Monk said, "It does no harm; simply let go and you will find peace. I then prostrated myself.
One day, while sitting quietly in the hall, I heard the clamor of a flock of geese from the place where they were released, ringing in my ears.
In the midst [of this], the three true dharmas manifest simultaneously; the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly do not arise.
The following day, he went to the abbot’s quarters to report his realization. The Old Monk said, "The previous were all states of consciousness; this is the state of wisdom. You must protect it well.
He then presented him with a verse: "With each entry, one becomes more intimate; What prevents you from turning back again at that intimate place? Thoroughly..."
When one reaches the bottom and exhausts the source, what is there? Beneath the eyebrows has always been the eye. I prostrated and withdrew.
On another day, the Old Monk addressed the assembly, citing the question posed by Layman Pang to Mazu: "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
Mazu replied, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River in a single mouth, and then I will tell you."
Later, when Pang Daowu arrived at Caotang, Qing took up the case and said: "Where have all these fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs gone? The Old Monk [Caotang] said:
"Everyone, try to provide a turning word for Mazu on behalf of him under Caotang’s statement.
I then gave a shout. After everyone had finished offering their words, the Old Monk spoke again: "Everyone is capable of acting for Mazu..."
He sighed. "In my view, even Mazu’s words only reach eighty percent. Is there anyone who can speak with ninety-nine percent perfection?
When Yu’s own response did not accord with the Master's intent, he was rebuked by the old monk and sent out. Returning to his quarters that night, he could find no peace.
As he was about to withdraw, he rolled up the curtain and stepped out of the hall. In a state of profound bewilderment, he suddenly crashed through the stone gate.

Thereupon, his mind opened wide and clear; all confusion dissolved like melting ice. He immediately blurted out a verse: "I cannot weep, nor can I laugh; I have struck blind my mother’s two natural eyes.
If someone asks me for the meaning of the West, I strike their face with my fist—no distinction between stranger or kin. Furthermore:
He said: "Within the light of fierce flames, a wooden horse flies; if you find it, mount it immediately. When the moment arrives, face-to-face, there is no turning back;
if you hesitate, you lose him at the very edge of the blade. He spoke again: "Dharma after dharma is the original Dharma; both rejecting and not rejecting cause injury.
Just as one wishes to bring the Way to full perfection, one does not realize that frost already fills the mouth. The next day, he went together with his fellow practitioners.
Mingyi went to the Abbot’s quarters to pay his respects and said, "I have a ten-part saying today that I would like to present to the Master.
The Old Master said, "Try to speak it for me. Mingyi turned his back, crossed his hands, and said to the Old Master, "I pray the Master will examine it.
The Old Master said, "A fine seven strokes of the rattan for you! Mingyi then prostrated himself and once again presented the previous three [cases].
The verse was recited. The Old Monk nodded in approval and then instructed him, saying: "This matter is high without a summit and deep without a bottom.
One cannot enter the measureless Dharma with a mind of limited measure. It must be through the complete purification of all things that one can finally maintain it with confidence.
I then bowed twice and received this instruction upon my head. Later, the Master would occasionally bring forth the essential principles of Dongshan to show them to me.
I answered each question with a verse, and in every case, our minds merged in perfect accord. At that time, I was already thirty-eight years old.

The following year, I took my leave and returned to Guangfu Hermitage in Jianning, where I closed my quarters for three years, secretly refining myself in meditation and earnestly seeking to sever all ties with the mundane world.
The Old Master then sent me a letter of admonition, saying: "The Buddha-dharma is on the verge of extinction; you must exert yourself and not [fail]."
He withdrew of his own accord due to the hardships of the times. Furthermore, encountering banditry and turmoil, he passed through the pass and went up the mountain to visit the Old Master.
The Old Master said, "I have long awaited your arrival," and he ordered him to return to the hall. For three years, he refined him daily, providing profound support for his realization of wisdom.
In the year of Dingsyou of the Shunzhi era, when the Old Master reached the age of eighty, on the first day of the first month, the Yuanxiao Festival—
He struck the bell to assemble the congregation and presented them with the *saṃghāṭī* robe and fly-whisk he had worn throughout his life. He spoke a verse, saying:
"Once I passed over the Shouchang Bridge; How could I follow worldly customs and give rise to trivial branches? With a single strand of hair, I wish to preserve the lineage of the thousand sages."
How many people can truly understand this mind? In my declining years, I am now eighty. At this very moment, the Great Matter is entrusted to you.
Regarding the matters of salt and sauce over thirty years, the ancients spoke these words without deception: "To steer against the wind requires the strength of a thousand *qun*;
only then can the foundation of eternal peace be firmly established. Because the grace of the Dharma-milk is so deep, I have exerted myself to respectfully receive [this transmission]. Immediately—

He was ordered daily to preside over the assembly and hold the whisk (*bifú*). Whenever it was a seasonal festival or the end of the year, he would invariably ascend the seat on his behalf to address the assembly.
Observing his expositions and proclamations, the Elder never failed to beat time with his hand and praise them as excellent. In the tenth month of winter, the Elder passed away.

In the first month of the following year, after the interment in the stupa was completed, the patrons Fang Gong Kechi and Lin Gong Kongshuo led the assembly of Dharma protectors, lay believers, and various others...
At Mount Sannō, the assembly insistently compelled me to succeed to the seat and open the Dharma. This was on the twenty-second day of the first month of the Wuxu year;
I was forty-four years of age. I resided there for fourteen years. Although there were often five thousand followers surrounding my seat, I felt ashamed that I had no Dharma to bestow upon them;
I merely established karmic conditions through the offering of rice and gruel. Reaching the autumn of the Xinhai year, I grew weary of receiving visitors. Just as I was...
When the Dharma-nephew Shichao Ning entered the mountains to pay his respects, he consulted with Master Lin Kongshuo, saying:
"In the past, the Elder Boshan opened the Dharma here on this mountain; Xueguan succeeded him, and our late teacher restored it.

I am unworthy to have followed in his footsteps, and although the Wanderer Lang once resided here, there has been no one since to succeed him. Now, Master Ning is his true heir; I pray that you will invite him."
He succeeded to the seat in order to continue the single lineage of Master Lang. I was weary of serving as a bridge for others, and thus I was able to retire; this was due to the Master’s grace.
The Master joyfully took up the responsibility with all his strength. I then spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, saying: "I am originally a guest without a home."
I remained on this mountain following circumstances for fourteen years. Suddenly, moved by inspiration, I departed through the Pine Pass; that very day, I shook off my robes and left.

The entire community wept and sought to detain me, but it was impossible. They pursued me as far as Taijiang before desisting. Master Ning, seeing that the sentiments of the assembly were divided, also did not succeed in staying.
Consequently, I was able to resign from my duties, which deeply satisfied my long-held aspirations. At that time, my age was already...
I am now fifty-seven years old. Upon arriving in Jianzhou, I was again detained by the assembly; there, I planted grass and gathered sand to perform the "empty-flower" Buddhist rites.
From then on, I styled myself a "wandering monk," drifting about according to circumstances with no fixed dwelling, like white clouds.
Whether it be Kaiyuan, Guangfu, or the various sites around Jinghu, all were places where I traveled back and forth with my staff. Later, I arrived at Baofu in Donghe and there I halted my carriage.

Because several years had passed since I first left the mountains, the great assembly within the mountain community frequently sent letters from the Sangha and the Dharma protectors urgently requesting my return.
These messages came in a constant stream along the roads. I excused myself, saying, "At seventy, one does not..."
I suppressed my breath and thought, "It is time to return. In the blink of an eye, I had unconsciously reached the age of seventy.
Furthermore, Master Jing retired from his duties, and the two superintendents, Chunyi and Yimai, passed away simultaneously.

With the mountain gate left without a master, the assembly of Dharma-protecting monks invoked our former agreement and pressured me to return to the mountain. For two or three years, they arrived in a continuous stream, leaving me no choice but to comply.
I have delayed for some time; it was only because of this aged and infirm body that I yielded myself to others and ventured here in my audacity.
It was the twenty-second day of the fourth month of the Jiazi year of the Kangxi era. Returning to the mountain, I ascended the hall: atop the towering peaks lies a single sheet of cloud;
riding the wind, it flies away and then flies back. To bring forth dews and rains is but a trivial matter—it provokes the laughter of the void.
Man-sae said: "I have long harbored the wish not to construct a separate stupa. This is because I do not wish to waste the blood and sweat of the faithful donors upon a putrid skull.
If I pass away on this mountain, let my remains be transported for cremation according to the standard protocol for deceased monks;

Do not move it; this is my most earnest exhortation. It must not be violated. I have a *Bingfu Lu* (Record of Holding the Whisk) in one fascicle from Gushan;

Tianning Tiri Gong of Yanzhen entered the monastic order in his youth and immediately encountered a spiritual mentor.
He realized there was a great matter in the Chan school and studied it in secret with diligent perseverance, never flagging even as he reached his sixtieth year; his resolve did not diminish.
Whenever he ascended Mount Gu at Drum Mountain to seek instruction, one day, while reading the *Record of Returning to the Mountains*, he experienced great joy and immediately—
Xue Rui led his disciples, together with his grand-disciple Jiefei, who jointly donated their robes and alms bowls to request that this work be carved into woodblocks for circulation.

In the past, at Mount Himavat, they sacrificed their bodies, and at Gandhamādana, they shattered their bones, seeking the Great Dharma; this was surely because they first gave rise to this single thought of delighting in the Dharma. Carved.

Postscript:

Great Master Weilín of Gǔshān donned the robe of gentleness and forbearance and entered the chamber of compassion. Seated upon the throne of the emptiness of dharmas, he expounded the Dharma for over thirty years.
Under his guidance, there were always five thousand followers who he led with steady and skillful instruction, like an aged [sage].
Affectionate toward his disciples as if they were his own children, he humbly delivered sentient beings like a bridge across a ford; truly, the Great Master was the most supple person in the world.
Yet, when upholding the seal of the school within his inner chamber, discerning demons from the authentic, he stood as immovable as a cliff ten thousand fathoms high;

What is called "extreme gentleness toward the Great Master" does not mean being weak or feeble;
it means being harmonious, mild, virtuous, and compliant, rather than abrupt or violent. What is called "extreme strength toward the Great Master" does not mean being forceful;
it means being harmonious without drifting, standing in the middle without leaning to either side. Yet these are all descriptions of the Great Master given in accordance with worldly convention.
Furthermore, if one were to discuss this according to the actual reality, then the Great Master was both flexible and firm, yet neither flexible nor firm;
he was a man of immeasurable capacity, a great guide who transcended all schools and surpassed all conventional standards.

He did not regard the adherence to a single mechanism or a single state as final realization, unlike those petty men within the Dharma-gate who act like thieves and burglars—harsh in appearance but weak within, outwardly...

He manifests the appearance of a great man, yet internally he lacks the preservation of the Dharma. Like children who consume things for the sake of power and profit, he casts aside his robes and whisk like so much dirt.
He has truly brought disorder to his own lineage while falsely claiming to maintain a strict tradition.

Record. In years past, I dispatched this record to the capital for printing. That I have now once again carved these blocks without negligence is because the single thread of the orthodox lineage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs today depends entirely upon the words and deeds of this Great Master.

My factionalism: though that which I do not side with is private interest and personal emotion, that which I cannot help but side with is rectitude and public principle.
Thus, even in a single phrase or a solitary word, my expressions shall be free from shame.
